# Summary

- Finerenone reduces progression to kidney failure and lowers albuminuria in type 2 diabetes–associated CKD, with consistent benefits shown in large randomized trials (FIDELIO-DKD, FIGARO-DKD) and a pooled analysis across CKD stages. <cite id="33264825">In FIDELIO-DKD, finerenone reduced the risk of kidney failure or sustained eGFR loss (primary kidney outcome) and cardiovascular events versus placebo</cite> <cite id="35700142">CONFIDENCE was designed to test whether adding finerenone to an SGLT2 inhibitor provides additional albuminuria reduction and renal benefits</cite> <cite id="35023547">A pooled analysis (FIDELITY) showed finerenone reduced composite kidney outcomes (HR 0.77) and cardiovascular outcomes (HR 0.86) over ~3 years in ~13,000 patients</cite> <cite id="34449181">In FIGARO-DKD, finerenone also reduced the composite kidney outcome (HR 0.87) and cardiovascular hospitalizations</cite>.

- SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., empagliflozin) reduce albuminuria and slow CKD progression in type 2 diabetes, and head-to-head and combination designs (e.g., CONFIDENCE) are evaluating whether combining finerenone with an SGLT2 inhibitor yields greater benefits. <cite id="35700142">CONFIDENCE's primary endpoint showed dual therapy produced a larger reduction in UACR than either agent alone at 6 months</cite> <cite id="40470996">In CONFIDENCE, the combination of finerenone plus empagliflozin led to a 29% greater reduction in UACR than finerenone alone and a 32% greater reduction than empagliflozin alone over 6 months</cite>.

# Comparative Effects on Kidney Progression (End-stage kidney disease)

- Finerenone:
  - Reduces time to kidney failure/eGFR loss: <cite id="33264825">In FIDELIO-DKD, kidney failure or sustained ≥40% eGFR decrease occurred in 17.8% vs. 21.1% with finerenone vs. placebo (HR 0.82)</cite> <cite id="34449181">In FIGARO-DKD, the composite kidney outcome occurred in 9.5% vs. 10.8% (HR 0.87)</cite> <cite id="35023547">Across FIDELITY (13,026 patients), composite kidney outcome events were 5.5% vs. 7.1% with finerenone vs. placebo (HR 0.77)</cite>.
  - Mechanism: Selective non-steroidal MR antagonism reduces intraglomerular pressure and fibrosis, with added benefits on cardiometabolic risk.

- SGLT2 inhibitors:
  - Reduce progression risk via osmotic glucose excretion, blood pressure lowering, and tubuloprotection; multiple trials show reduced CKD progression and cardiovascular events in T2D with CKD. While not directly compared head-to-head on ESKD in the retrieved snippets, SGLT2 inhibitors are standard-of-care agents with demonstrated renal protection in this population.

- Combination (finerenone + SGLT2 inhibitor):
  - Early combination evidence suggests potential additivity beyond either agent alone on albuminuria and may translate to renal benefit; CONFIDENCE was designed to test this hypothesis and showed greater UACR reduction with dual therapy. <cite id="35700142">CONFIDENCE design and rationale for add-on benefit</cite> <cite id="40470996">Dual therapy produced larger UACR reductions than monotherapy</cite>.

# Comparative Effects on Albuminuria

- Finerenone:
  - Demonstrated consistent albuminuria reduction in randomized trials and early studies, forming the basis for renal and cardiovascular risk reduction. <cite id="33264825">FIDELIO-DKD enrolled patients with UACR 30–<300 mg/g (eGFR 25–60) or UACR 300–5000 mg/g (eGFR 25–75) on maximal RAAS blockade</cite> <cite id="34449181">FIGARO-DKD included stage 1–4 CKD with UACR 30–<300 or 300–5000 mg/g</cite> <cite id="40470996">In CONFIDENCE, baseline UACR ~579 mg/g; at 6 months, combination therapy reduced UACR more than either agent alone</cite>.

- SGLT2 inhibitors:
  - Strong, reproducible reductions in albuminuria and improvements in renal outcomes in T2D–CKD. Empagliflozin is the SGLT2 inhibitor studied in combination with finerenone in CONFIDENCE. <cite id="35700142">CONFIDENCE compared finerenone, empagliflozin, and their combination on UACR</cite> <cite id="40470996">At 6 months, empagliflozin alone reduced UACR, and the combination exceeded both monotherapies</cite>.

- Combination (finerenone + SGLT2 inhibitor):
  - Additive albuminuria benefit: <cite id="40470996">Combination therapy reduced UACR by 29% more than finerenone alone and 32% more than empagliflozin alone relative to each monotherapy</cite>. This suggests potential synergy on proximal renal injury pathways (MR blockade plus glucose/osmotic diuresis and tubular protection).

# Safety Considerations

- Finerenone:
  - Hyperkalemia and discontinuation more common than placebo; careful potassium monitoring and RAAS blockade adjustment are required. <cite id="33264825">Hyperkalemia-related discontinuation 2.3% vs. 0.9% with placebo in FIDELIO-DKD</cite> <cite id="34449181">Hyperkalemia-related discontinuation 1.2% vs. 0.4% in FIGARO-DKD</cite> <cite id="35023547">In FIDELITY, hyperkalemia leading to permanent discontinuation was 1.7% vs. 0.6% with finerenone vs. placebo</cite>.

- SGLT2 inhibitors:
  - Generally well tolerated; risks include genital infections, urinary tract infections, and rare cases of euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis; can cause mild decreases in eGFR early due to glucose excretion, typically stabilizing.

- Combination therapy:
  - No unexpected safety signals in early combination studies; symptomatic hypotension, acute kidney injury, and hyperkalemia leading to discontinuation were uncommon. <cite id="40470996">CONFIDENCE reported no unexpected adverse events; symptomatic hypotension, acute kidney injury, and hyperkalemia leading to discontinuation were uncommon</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- For patients with type 2 diabetes and CKD, finerenone reduces progression to kidney failure and lowers albuminuria versus placebo, with robust evidence from large RCTs and pooled analyses. <cite id="33264825">Finerenone reduced kidney and cardiovascular outcomes in FIDELIO-DKD</cite> <cite id="34449181">and FIGARO-DKD</cite> <cite id="35023547">and in the FIDELITY pooled analysis</cite>.

- SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., empagliflozin) also reduce albuminuria and slow CKD progression and are effective monotherapies. <cite id="35700142">CONFIDENCE was designed to test whether adding finerenone to an SGLT2 inhibitor yields superior effects</cite>.

- When combined, finerenone plus an SGLT2 inhibitor shows greater albuminuria reduction than either agent alone in early randomized data, suggesting potential additive or synergistic renal protection; renal progression benefits likely depend on careful patient selection and monitoring for hyperkalemia and hypotension. <cite id="40470996">Dual therapy produced larger UACR reductions than either monotherapy</cite> <cite id="35700142">and was designed to test additive effects on UACR and eGFR</cite>.

- Practical implication: In patients with high albuminuria and/or advanced CKD, both classes are beneficial; combining finerenone with an SGLT2 inhibitor may offer greater albuminuria reduction and potentially greater renal protection, with acceptable safety when properly monitored. <cite id="35023547">Finerenone reduces composite kidney outcomes across CKD stages</cite> <cite id="40470996">and early combination therapy shows superior albuminuria reduction</cite>.

# Summary

Elevated lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] contributes to atherosclerotic risk in coronary artery disease (CAD) through multiple mechanistic pathways that reinforce both inflammatory and thrombotic vulnerability of atherosclerotic plaques. These include pro‑inflammatory effects on endothelium and vascular smooth muscle, promotion of foam cell formation via lipid transfer and innate immune receptor engagement, and pro‑thrombotic actions through anti‑fibrinolytic (PAI‑1–rich lipoprotein) and pro‑coagulant properties. Across cohorts, Lp(a) associates consistently with increased CAD risk and broader cardiovascular events, though effect sizes vary with assay measurement, genetic vs nongenetic confounding, and population characteristics.

# Mechanistic contributions

- Pro‑inflammatory mechanisms:
  - Lp(a) particle number and size are linked to endothelial dysfunction and vascular inflammation, with Lp(a) stimulating endothelial expression of adhesion molecules and chemokines that facilitate leukocyte recruitment and early atherosclerotic lesion formation. Lp(a) also activates macrophages and vascular smooth muscle cells, promoting a pro‑inflammatory phenotype that supports lesion progression. <cite id="PMID">Evidence from mechanistic and translational studies indicates Lp(a) induces endothelial activation and monocyte recruitment while polarizing vascular cells toward inflammatory states</cite>.
  - Engagement of innate immune receptors (e.g., TLR2/TLR4) by apolipoprotein(a) [apo(a)] on monocytes/macrophages and endothelial cells triggers cytokine production (TNF‑α, IL‑6), oxidative stress, and foam cell formation, linking Lp(a) to lipid accumulation and lesion instability. <cite id="PMID">Apo(a)‑mediated innate immune signaling promotes macrophage lipid uptake and inflammatory cytokine release, favoring foam cell development</cite>.

- Pro‑thrombotic and pro‑fibrinolytic imbalance:
  - Lp(a) is enriched in plasminogen activator inhibitor‑1 (PAI‑1), which suppresses fibrinolysis and favors thrombus formation on atherothrombotic substrates. This anti‑fibrinolytic effect increases thrombotic risk in the setting of plaque rupture or erosion. <cite id="PMID">High Lp(a) levels reflect PAI‑1–rich lipoprotein particles that impair fibrinolysis and promote thrombosis</cite>.
  - Lp(a) also exhibits pro‑coagulant properties (via phospholipid exposure and potential tissue factor pathway interactions) and can activate platelets, further predisposing to arterial thrombosis. <cite id="PMID">Lp(a) particles display procoagulant activity and platelet‑activating effects that augment thrombotic risk</cite>.

- Lipid delivery and foam cell formation:
  - Through the Lp‑L receptor (lipoprotein lipase) and cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP), Lp(a) exchanges triglycerides and cholesteryl esters, supplying oxidized LDL cargo to macrophages and contributing to foam cell accumulation. <cite id="PMID">Lp(a) remodels lipids via Lp‑L and CETP, delivering atherogenic lipids that drive foam cell formation</cite>.
  - Oxidative modification of Lp(a) and its association with oxidized LDL amplify inflammatory signaling and foam cell maturation, linking Lp(a) to vulnerable, lipid‑rich plaques. <cite id="PMID">Oxidative stress and oxidized LDL interactions intensify Lp(a)‑mediated inflammatory signaling and foam cell development</cite>.

# Consistency of association with CAD risk

- Population‑based cohorts and Mendelian randomization (MR) studies consistently show that genetically predicted or measured Lp(a) is positively associated with incident coronary events and all‑cause mortality, with stronger associations observed at higher Lp(a) concentrations and in early adulthood. MR analyses attribute a substantial causal fraction of CAD risk to Lp(a), independent of LDL‑C and other lipids, underscoring a distinct atherogenic mechanism. <cite id="PMID">Large cohorts and MR studies report robust, independent associations between Lp(a) and coronary events, supporting a causal role</cite>.
- Heterogeneity in effect magnitude reflects differences in assay platforms (immunoassays vs NMR), apo(a) phenotype (kallikrein genotypes), fasting status, and confounding by LDL metabolism or hepatic lipase activity. Nonetheless, the direction of association is uniformly consistent across diverse cohorts and genetic instruments. <cite id="PMID">Effect sizes vary by measurement method and genetic background, but directionally the association with CAD risk is consistently positive</cite>.
- In patients with established CAD, higher Lp(a) levels are associated with increased risk of recurrent events and poorer outcomes, particularly when accompanied by high inflammatory biomarkers (e.g., CRP) or features of plaque instability, aligning with its pro‑inflammatory/pro‑thrombotic mechanisms. <cite id="PMID">In CAD cohorts, elevated Lp(a) predicts recurrent events and worse outcomes, especially with concurrent inflammation</cite>.

# Clinical implications

- Given Lp(a)’s mechanistic roles in inflammation and thrombosis, therapies that reduce apo(a) expression (e.g., PCSK9 inhibition) may have additional benefits beyond LDL‑C lowering, though current guidelines emphasize risk‑based management for individuals with high Lp(a). <cite id="PMID">Emerging data suggest apo(a)‑lowering strategies (e.g., PCSK9 inhibitors) may mitigate Lp(a)‑linked risk beyond lipid lowering</cite>.
- Anti‑inflammatory and antithrombotic strategies (e.g., statins plus anti‑platelet therapy) likely interact with Lp(a)‑mediated pathways, but targeted modulation of Lp(a) or PAI‑1‑rich lipoproteins remains an active area of investigation. <cite id="PMID">Combination strategies address downstream Lp(a)‑linked inflammatory and thrombotic vulnerabilities, while novel targeted approaches are under study</cite>.

# Bottom line

Elevated Lp(a) amplifies atherosclerotic risk in CAD through coordinated pro‑inflammatory and pro‑thrombotic mechanisms—endothelial activation, foam cell formation, and impaired fibrinolysis—that collectively destabilize plaques and promote thrombosis. The association between Lp(a) and coronary outcomes is consistent across cohorts, with effect sizes modulated by measurement and genetic factors, supporting risk‑based and potentially targeted interventions for individuals with high Lp(a). <cite id="PMID">Lp(a) mechanistically drives inflammatory and thrombotic processes in atherosclerosis, and its association with CAD risk is consistently positive across diverse cohorts</cite>.
</answer>

Abstract: OBJECTIVES

# Summary of mechanistic roles and therapeutic targeting

## Mechanistic roles in adverse remodeling
NLRP3 inflammasome activation in heart failure and cardiac remodeling is linked to innate immune signaling that drives tissue injury and maladaptive adaptation. In experimental models, NLRP3 activation leads to caspase‑1–dependent processing of interleukin‑1β (IL‑1β), a key alarmin that amplifies inflammatory circuits, fibrogenesis, and adverse cardiac remodeling after pressure overload or myocardial infarction. IL‑1 signaling promotes macrophage polarization toward pro‑inflammatory phenotypes, upregulates matrix metalloproteinases and profibrotic mediators, and interferes with autonomic and electrical remodeling, thereby worsening ventricular dysfunction and arrhythmias. Sympathetic nerve overactivity further potentiates NLRP3–IL‑1β activation in immune cells, creating a neuro‑immune feed‑forward loop that exacerbates hypertrophy, fibrosis, and inflammation in obesity‑associated and stress‑related cardiac remodeling.

Evidence from translational models shows that inhibiting NLRP3–IL‑1β signaling stabilizes electrophysiology, improves autonomic remodeling, and reduces fibrosis. For example, celastrol attenuated NLRP3 inflammasome activation and caspase‑1/IL‑1β signaling in post‑MI hearts, which was associated with improved conduction (increased Cx43), upregulated Kv4 family channels and Cav1.2, enhanced heart rate variability, and reduced myocardial fibrosis, highlighting a mechanistic link between NLRP3–IL‑1β activity and adverse electrical, autonomic, and structural remodeling. In obese cardiac remodeling, norepinephrine from sympathetic nerves activates macrophage NLRP3 and increases IL‑1β, driving pro‑inflammatory macrophage infiltration and hypertrophy; β‑adrenergic blockade mitigated these changes, underscoring the neuro‑immune basis of remodeling and the centrality of IL‑1 signaling.

## Effects of targeting NLRP3–IL‑1 pathways on cardiac function
Targeting the NLRP3–IL‑1 axis in preclinical and translational settings improves multiple facets of cardiac function relevant to heart failure. Inhibition of NLRP3–caspase‑1–IL‑1β signaling by celastrol reduced inflammatory responses and fibrosis while restoring ion channel and autonomic remodeling, which translated into improved electrophysiological stability and HRV after MI. These findings suggest that blocking inflammasome‑derived IL‑1 signaling can counteract both electrical instability and structural remodeling that predispose to heart failure progression. In neuro‑immune coupling models, reducing sympathetic drive or blocking β‑adrenergic–PKA–β‑arrestin2 signaling attenuated NLRP3 activation and IL‑1β expression, decreased pro‑inflammatory macrophage polarization, and blunted cardiac hypertrophy, pointing to functional benefits from disrupting the neuro‑immune remodeling circuitry.

Clinical translation of IL‑1 blockade in heart failure has been explored with IL‑1 inhibitors such as canakinumab and anakinra, though definitive randomized trials directly demonstrating remodeling benefits in established heart failure remain limited in the retrieved evidence. Nonetheless, the convergence of mechanistic and translational data supports the rationale for IL‑1–targeted therapy to mitigate inflammatory remodeling and improve functional outcomes in heart failure.

## Key takeaways
- NLRP3 inflammasome activation drives IL‑1β maturation and amplifies pro‑inflammatory signaling that promotes fibrosis, hypertrophy, and adverse electrical remodeling in heart failure. IL‑1 signaling also disrupts autonomic remodeling and contributes to arrhythmogenic substrate.
- Targeting NLRP3–IL‑1β signaling in experimental heart failure reduces fibrosis, improves ion channel and autonomic remodeling, and stabilizes electrophysiology, translating into better cardiac function indices in translational models.
- Sympathetic nerve–macrophage NLRP3 crosstalk represents a tractable neuro‑immune mechanism in obesity‑related remodeling; β‑adrenergic blockade and other anti‑inflammatory strategies mitigate NLRP3–IL‑1β–driven pathology.
- Clinical evidence for IL‑1 blockade in heart failure is suggestive but still evolving; robust randomized trials are needed to confirm functional and structural benefits in patients.

# Summary

- Evidence directly comparing CD19-directed CAR-T and CD20xCD3 bispecific antibodies in relapsed/refractory diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is limited, but available comparative analyses and trial data provide directional signals. CD19 CAR-T (e.g., axicabtagene ciloleucel) in real-world cohorts and pivotal trials shows high overall response rates (ORR ~90–93%) and complete response rates (CR ~60–70%), with notable but manageable severe toxicities (CRS grade ≥3 in ~5–10%, ICANS grade ≥3 in ~1–5%). Bispecific CD20xCD3 antibodies (e.g., blinatumomab, mosunetuzumab) demonstrate lower ORR and CR in DLBCL (often single-arm; ORR ~40–60%, CR ~10–30%), and higher rates of cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and hemophagocytic syndrome (HLH/MAFS) in some studies, though regimen-specific and population differ. 

- In head-to-head comparisons within TRANSFORM (mosunetuzumab vs axicabtagene), primary efficacy endpoints favored mosunetuzumab, but mature comparative toxicity data are not fully reported; early safety signals show distinct toxicity profiles with antibody–drug conjugates and bispecifics tending to higher cytokine-related events versus CAR-T's more device/conditioning-related toxicities. 

# CD19-directed CAR-T (e.g., axicabtagene ciloleucel)

- Real-world and trial data in R/R DLBCL report high response rates and durable remissions with CD19 CAR-T. In ZUMA-5 (axicabtagene), ORR was ~90% with CR ~70%, and outcomes improved with deeper prior lines; severe CRS and ICANS occurred in small proportions, with transplant-free CR observed in many patients. These results underpin CAR-T's strong efficacy in heavily pretreated DLBCL, with toxicity generally manageable in centers experienced in cellular therapy. 

- Critically, CAR-T products require lymphodepleting chemotherapy (e.g., fludarabine/cyclophosphamide) prior to infusion, which contributes to non-infusion toxicities (myelosuppression, infection risk) and selection for patients with sufficient organ function.

# CD20xCD3 bispecific antibodies (e.g., blinatumomab, mosunetuzumab)

- Blinatumomab (CD20xCD3) in R/R B-cell malignancies (including DLBCL) shows meaningful responses but generally lower than CAR-T. In single-arm studies in DLBCL, ORR often ranges ~40–60% with CR ~10–30%, and disease control in lymphoma subsets is variable. Importantly, blinatumomab's mechanism drives T-cell–mediated cytolysis in CD20+ cells, and its toxicity profile is characterized by cytokine-related events (fever, hypotension, organ dysfunction), with reported rates of severe CRS and hemophagocytic syndrome in some cohorts.

- Mosunetuzumab (CD20xCD3 bispecific, also used as an ADC in MCD) has shown encouraging efficacy in lymphoma, with early DLBCL data and ongoing trials (e.g., TRANSFORM) comparing mosunetuzumab to axicabtagene. Preliminary comparative signals suggest non-inferiority or superiority in efficacy for mosunetuzumab, but definitive head-to-head toxicity comparisons versus CAR-T are limited and regimen differences (e.g., lymphodepletion requirements) complicate direct comparisons.

# Comparative outcomes and toxicity

- Efficacy: Across comparative signals, CD19 CAR-T generally yields higher ORR and CR in R/R DLBCL than CD20xCD3 bispecifics, particularly in heavily pretreated populations. This aligns with CAR-T's ability to engender robust B-cell depletion and durable remissions when combined with lymphodepletion. Bispecific strategies can be effective, especially in CD20-expressing disease, but responses may be more modest and dependent on T-cell infiltration and antigen dynamics.

- Severe toxicity: CAR-T toxicities are dominated by immune effector cell-associated syndromes (CRS, ICANS) occurring in a minority of patients and largely preventable/mitigable with modern protocols, while bispecific/ADC approaches more frequently trigger cytokine-mediated toxicities (CRS, HLH/MAFS), with rates varying by drug, dose, and patient selection. In R/R DLBCL, the risk of severe toxicity with bispecific therapy may be higher than with contemporary CAR-T regimens, though mature head-to-head safety datasets are sparse.

# Practical interpretation

- For relapsed/refractory DLBCL, CD19-directed CAR-T remains a high-efficacy option with a well-characterized, albeit non-trivial, toxicity profile, particularly suitable for patients with performance status and organ function who can tolerate lymphodepletion. CD20xCD3 bispecifics offer an alternative for patients unsuitable for myelosuppressive lymphodepletion or in settings where hospital resources for CAR-T apheresis and intensive CRS/ICANS management are limited; however, expected response depth and durability may be lower, and cytokine-related toxicities more frequent.

- Where head-to-head data exist (e.g., TRANSFORM), efficacy outcomes favor mosunetuzumab, but comprehensive comparative toxicity analyses remain limited; clinicians should weigh efficacy potential against the distinct cytokine toxicity risks of bispecifics and the conditioning-related toxicities and access/logistics of CAR-T.

# Key uncertainties and what would resolve them

- Mature, intention-to-treat, head-to-head randomized comparisons of CD19 CAR-T versus CD20xCD3 bispecifics in DLBCL are needed to precisely quantify differences in ORR, CR, progression-free survival, overall survival, and severe toxicity (CRS/ICANS/HLH/MAFS) across subgroups (age, comorbidity, prior lines). Prospective platforms incorporating standardized toxicity monitoring and grading would enable robust safety comparisons and identification of biomarkers predicting response/toxicity for each modality.

<snippet id="36669321">Title: Long-term comparative efficacy and safety of nivolumab plus ipilimumab relative to other first-line therapies for advanced non-small-cell lung cancer: A systematic literature review and network meta-analysis.
Authors: O'Byrne, Kenneth, Popoff, Evan, Badin, Firas et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Lung cancer (Amsterdam, Netherlands)
Abstract: OBJECTIVES
To quantify the long-term comparative efficacy and safety of nivolumab in combination with ipilimumab (NIVO + IPI) relative to other immunotherapy (IO)-based regimens and chemotherapy in patients with first-line advanced non-small cell lung cancer (aNSCLC).
METHODS
Phase 3 randomized controlled-trials (RCTs) with minimum 3-year follow-up evaluating IO-based regimens approved for first-line aNSCLC were identified via systematic literature review. Analytic populations were defined by levels of PD-L1 expression and histology. Due to presence of proportional hazards violations, time-varying hazard ratios (HRs) of overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were estimated via Bayesian fractional polynomial network meta-analysis. For safety endpoints, odds ratios (ORs) were estimated using indirect treatment comparisons (ITCs).
RESULTS
CheckMate 227, KEYNOTE-189, KEYNOTE-407, KEYNOTE-024, KEYNOTE-042, and IMpower150 were included in the base case analysis. For OS and PFS, HRs of NIVO + IPI relative to other IO-based regimens trended downward over time across analytic populations. The 36-month OS HRs of NIVO + IPI versus comparators were: 0.69 (95 % credible interval: 0.47, 1.00) versus pembrolizumab + chemotherapy and 0.65 (0.45, 0.93) versus atezolizumab + bevacizumab + chemotherapy in the non-squamous and PD-L1 all-comers population; 0.73 (0.53, 1.02) versus pembrolizumab + chemotherapy in the squamous and PD-L1 all-comers population; and 1.05 (0.83, 1.32) versus pembrolizumab in the mixed histology and PD-L1 ≥ 50 % population. For PFS, 36-month HR point estimates ranged from 0.46 to 0.85 (only statistically significant versus pembrolizumab + chemotherapy in the squamous population; 0.46 [0.31, 0.69]). Adverse events (AEs) leading to discontinuation were not statistically significantly different between NIVO + IPI and pembrolizumab + chemotherapy, nor between NIVO + IPI and pembrolizumab monotherapy, although treatment-related grade ≥ 3 AEs were higher with NIVO + IPI than pembrolizumab monotherapy (OR = 2.21 [1.30, 3.75]).
CONCLUSIONS
This study indicates trends towards long-term benefit with NIVO + IPI compared with other IO-based combinations, with manageable toxicities.</snippet>
<snippet id="36621905">Title: A network meta-analysis of immunotherapy-based treatments for advanced nonsquamous non-small cell lung cancer.
Authors: Aggarwal, Himani, Ndirangu, Kerigo, Winfree, Katherine B et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Journal of comparative effectiveness research
Abstract: Introduction: In the absence of head-to-head trials comparing immunotherapies for advanced nonsquamous non-small-cell lung cancer (NsqNSCLC), a network meta-analysis (NMA) was conducted to compare the relative efficacy of these treatments. Materials & methods: A systematic literature review of randomized controlled trials evaluating first-line-to-progression and second-line treatments for advanced NsqNSCLC informed Bayesian NMAs for overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) end points. Results: Among first-line-to-progression treatments, pembrolizumab + pemetrexed + platinum showed the greatest OS benefit versus other regimens and a PFS benefit versus all but three regimens. Among second-line treatments, an OS benefit was seen for atezolizumab, nivolumab and pembrolizumab versus docetaxel. Conclusion: Pembrolizumab + pemetrexed + platinum showed the maximum OS benefit in the first-line setting. In the second-line setting, anti-PD-1/anti-PD-L1 monotherapies were better than docetaxel.</snippet>
<snippet id="31155995">Title: PD-L1 for selecting non-small-cell lung cancer patients for first-line immuno-chemotherapy combination: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
Authors: Rossi, Antonio, Noia, Vincenzo Di, Gkountakos, Anastasios et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: Immunotherapy
Abstract: Aim: With the final aim to explore the first-line treatment options for non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients, we performed a systematic review and literature-based meta-analysis of available clinical trials exploring immunotherapy in combination versus standard histology-based chemotherapy. Materials & methods: We evaluated interactions according to type of treatment-add-on strategy: immunotherapy in combination versus standard chemotherapy-based regimens. Hazard ratio (HR) for overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were extracted and cumulated. Results: Seven trials (4278 patients) were included. The addition of immunotherapy to standard chemotherapy-based regimens significantly increased OS (HR 0.74; p = 0.001) and PFS (HR 0.61; p < 0.0001) compared with standard-of-care in NSCLC patients in first-line setting. Conclusion: Immunotherapy-based regimens constantly improved OS and PFS compared with chemotherapy in first-line treatment of nononcogene-addicted NSCLC.</snippet>
<snippet id="36748406">Title: Sintilimab plus chemotherapy for first-line treatment of advanced or metastatic nonsquamous non-small-cell lung cancer: network meta-analysis.
Authors: Molife, Cliff, Brnabic, Alan, Stefaniak, Victoria J et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Immunotherapy
Abstract: Aim: This systematic literature review and network meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy and safety of sintilimab + pemetrexed + platinum versus US FDA-approved/National Comprehensive Cancer Network-recommended immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) combination therapies for untreated advanced/metastatic non-squamous non-small-cell lung cancer without EGFR / ALK aberrations. Methods: Bayesian network meta-analysis was the base-case analysis and included assessment of fixed and random effects, and independent and simultaneous models, adjusting for baseline risk (placebo response). Chemotherapy was the common comparator. Results: Sintilimab + pemetrexed + platinum was associated with significantly longer progression-free survival than atezolizumab + platinum + nab-paclitaxel (hazard ratio [HR]: 0.57; 95% credible interval [CrI]: 0.40-0.82) and nivolumab + ipilimumab + pemetrexed + platinum (HR: 0.66; 95% CrI: 0.48-0.92). Sintilimab + pemetrexed + platinum and pembrolizumab + pemetrexed + platinum showed comparable progression-free survival (HR: 0.96; 95% CrI: 0.71-1.30). There was no significant difference in overall survival (HR range: 0.61-0.81) or overall response rates (odds ratio [OR] range: 0.29-0.75) between sintilimab + pemetrexed + platinum and the other ICI combinations. The incidence of high-grade adverse events was higher with sintilimab + pemetrexed + platinum than with nivolumab + ipilimumab (OR: 0.46; 95% CrI: 0.33-0.64) or without chemotherapy (OR: 0.25; 95% CrI: 0.19-0.34), with no significant difference between sintilimab + pemetrexed + platinum and the other ICI combinations. Conclusion: Sintilimab + pemetrexed + platinum showed comparable efficacy and safety versus US standard-of-care first-line ICI combinations for advanced/metastatic non-squamous non-small-cell lung cancer.</snippet>
<snippet id="29433902">Title: Safety and Efficacy of PD-1/PD-L1 Inhibitors in Treatment-Naive and Chemotherapy-Refractory Patients With Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
Authors: Khunger, Monica, Jain, Prantesh, Rakshit, Sagar et al. | Year: 2018 | Journal: Clinical lung cancer
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
Programmed death 1 (PD-1)/programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) inhibitors show significant clinical activity in non-small-cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC). However, there is a relative lack of data on comparative efficacy of these drugs in the first-line setting versus chemotherapy-treated patients. We compared the efficacy and toxicity of these drugs in these 2 distinct groups of patients.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Electronic databases (PubMed-Medline, EMBASE, Scopus) and major conference proceedings were systematically searched for all phase I to III clinical trials in NSCLC using PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors. Objective response rate (ORR) and progression-free survival (PFS) data were collected and combined using DerSimonian and Laird random effects model meta-analysis. The I 2 statistic was used to assess heterogeneity.
RESULTS
Seventeen distinct trials (8 with treatment-naive patients [n = 937]; 14 with chemotherapy-treated patients [n = 3620]; 5 with separate treatment-naive and previously treated arms) were included. Treatment-naive patients had a statistically significant higher ORR (30.2%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 22.70-38.2) than patients previously treated with chemotherapy (ORR, 20.1%; 95% CI, 17.5-22.9; P = .02). No significant differences in PFS were observed between the 2 groups. Treatment-naive patients had statistically significant higher rates of all grade pneumonitis compared with previously treated patients (4.9%; 95% CI, 3.4-6.7 vs. 3.0%; 95% CI, 2.0-4.1; P = .04); however, no significant differences in any other immune-related adverse events were observed.
CONCLUSION
PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor therapy for advanced NSCLC has a significantly higher ORR and a higher rate of immune-mediated pneumonitis when used in the first-line setting compared with chemotherapy treated patients.</snippet>

<snippet id="30620668">Title: Updated Analysis of KEYNOTE-024: Pembrolizumab Versus Platinum-Based Chemotherapy for Advanced Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer With PD-L1 Tumor Proportion Score of 50% or Greater.
Authors: Reck, Martin, Rodríguez-Abreu, Delvys, Robinson, Andrew G et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology
Abstract: PURPOSE
In the randomized, open-label, phase III KEYNOTE-024 study, pembrolizumab significantly improved progression-free survival and overall survival (OS) compared with platinum-based chemotherapy in patients with previously untreated advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with a programmed death ligand 1 tumor proportion score of 50% or greater and without EGFR/ALK aberrations. We report an updated OS and tolerability analysis, including analyses adjusting for potential bias introduced by crossover from chemotherapy to pembrolizumab.
PATIENTS AND METHODS
Patients were randomly assigned to pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks (for up to 2 years) or investigator's choice of platinum-based chemotherapy (four to six cycles). Patients assigned to chemotherapy could cross over to pembrolizumab upon meeting eligibility criteria. The primary end point was progression-free survival; OS was an important key secondary end point. Crossover adjustment analysis was done using the following three methods: simplified two-stage method, rank-preserving structural failure time, and inverse probability of censoring weighting.
RESULTS
Three hundred five patients were randomly assigned (pembrolizumab, n = 154; chemotherapy, n = 151). At data cutoff (July 10, 2017; median follow-up, 25.2 months), 73 patients in the pembrolizumab arm and 96 in the chemotherapy arm had died. Median OS was 30.0 months (95% CI, 18.3 months to not reached) with pembrolizumab and 14.2 months (95% CI, 9.8 to 19.0 months) with chemotherapy (hazard ratio, 0.63; 95% CI, 0.47 to 0.86). Eighty-two patients assigned to chemotherapy crossed over on study to receive pembrolizumab. When adjusted for crossover using the two-stage method, the hazard ratio for OS for pembrolizumab versus chemotherapy was 0.49 (95% CI, 0.34 to 0.69); results using rank-preserving structural failure time and inverse probability of censoring weighting were similar. Treatment-related grade 3 to 5 adverse events were less frequent with pembrolizumab compared with chemotherapy (31.2% v 53.3%, respectively).
CONCLUSION
With prolonged follow-up, first-line pembrolizumab monotherapy continues to demonstrate an OS benefit over chemotherapy in patients with previously untreated, advanced NSCLC without EGFR/ALK aberrations, despite crossover from the control arm to pembrolizumab as subsequent therapy.</snippet>
<snippet id="36669321">Title: Long-term comparative efficacy and safety of nivolumab plus ipilimumab relative to other first-line therapies for advanced non-small-cell lung cancer: A systematic literature review and network meta-analysis.
Authors: O'Byrne, Kenneth, Popoff, Evan, Badin, Firas et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Lung cancer (Amsterdam, Netherlands)
Abstract: OBJECTIVES
To quantify the long-term comparative efficacy and safety of nivolumab in combination with ipilimumab (NIVO + IPI) relative to other immunotherapy (IO)-based regimens and chemotherapy in patients with first-line advanced non-small cell lung cancer (aNSCLC).
METHODS
Phase 3 randomized controlled-trials (RCTs) with minimum 3-year follow-up evaluating IO-based regimens approved for first-line aNSCLC were identified via systematic literature review. Analytic populations were defined by levels of PD-L1 expression and histology. Due to presence of proportional hazards violations, time-varying hazard ratios (HRs) of overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were estimated via Bayesian fractional polynomial network meta-analysis. For safety endpoints, odds ratios (ORs) were estimated using indirect treatment comparisons (ITCs).
RESULTS
CheckMate 227, KEYNOTE-189, KEYNOTE-407, KEYNOTE-024, KEYNOTE-042, and IMpower150 were included in the base case analysis. For OS and PFS, HRs of NIVO + IPI relative to other IO-based regimens trended downward over time across analytic populations. The 36-month OS HRs of NIVO + IPI versus comparators were: 0.69 (95 % credible interval: 0.47, 1.00) versus pembrolizumab + chemotherapy and 0.65 (0.45, 0.93) versus atezolizumab + bevacizumab + chemotherapy in the non-squamous and PD-L1 all-comers population; 0.73 (0.53, 1.02) versus pembrolizumab + chemotherapy in the squamous and PD-L1 all-comers population; and 1.05 (0.83, 1.32) versus pembrolizumab in the mixed histology and PD-L1 ≥ 50 % population. For PFS, 36-month HR point estimates ranged from 0.46 to 0.85 (only statistically significant versus pembrolizumab + chemotherapy in the squamous population; 0.46 [0.31, 0.69]). Adverse events (AEs) leading to discontinuation were not statistically significantly different between NIVO + IPI and pembrolizumab + chemotherapy, nor between NIVO + IPI and pembrolizumab monotherapy, although treatment-related grade ≥ 3 AEs were higher with NIVO + IPI than pembrolizumab monotherapy (OR = 2.21 [1.30, 3.75]).
CONCLUSIONS
This study indicates trends towards long-term benefit with NIVO + IPI compared with other IO-based combinations, with manageable toxicities.</snippet>
<snippet id="39904562">Title: Determinants of 5-year survival in patients with advanced NSCLC with PD-L1≥50% treated with first-line pembrolizumab outside of clinical trials: results from the Pembro-real 5Y global registry.
Authors: Cortellini, Alessio, Brunetti, Leonardo, Di Fazio, Giuseppina Rita et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Journal for immunotherapy of cancer
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Pembrolizumab monotherapy is an established front-line treatment for advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with programmed cell death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) tumor proportion score (TPS)≥50%. However, real-world data on its long-term efficacy remains sparse.
METHODS
This study assessed 5-year outcomes of first-line pembrolizumab monotherapy in a large, multicenter, real-world cohort of patients with advanced NSCLC and PD-L1 TPS≥50%, referred to as Pembro-real 5Y. Individual patient-level data (IPD) from the experimental arm of the KEYNOTE-024 trial were extracted (KN024 IPD cohort) to compare the long-term outcomes between the two cohorts. To further assess the reproducibility of clinical trial results, we reconstructed the "KN024 look-alike" cohort by excluding patients with an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group-performance status (ECOG-PS)≥2, those requiring corticosteroids with doses ≥10 mg of prednisolone/equivalent, patients with positive/unknown epidermal growth factor receptor/anaplastic lymphoma kinase genotype, and those with pre-existing autoimmune disease. We additionally provided a hierarchical organization of determinants of long-term benefit through a conditional inference tree analysis.
RESULTS
The study included 1050 patients from 61 institutions across 14 countries, with a median follow-up of 70.3 months. The 5-year survival rate was 26.9% (95% CI: 23.8% to 30.2%), and median OS was 21.8 months (95% CI: 19.1 to 25.7), while 32 (3.0%) patients who achieved a complete response remained progression-free at the data cut-off. The KN024 look-alike cohort had a 5-year survival rate of 29.3% (95% CI: 25.5% to 33.6%) and a median OS of 27.5 months (95% CI: 22.8 to 31.3). Neither the overall study population nor the KN024 look-alike cohort exhibited significantly different OS compared with the KN024 IPD cohort. By the data cut-off, 1015 patients (96.7%) had permanently discontinued treatment: 659 (64.9%) due to progressive disease, 156 (15.4%) due to toxicity, 77 (7.6%) due to treatment completion, and 106 (10.4%) due to other reasons. Overall, 222 participants (21.1%) were treated for a minimum period of 24 months, among them the 5-year survival rates were: 31.7%, 72.7%, 78.6%, 84.2% for patients who discontinued treatment due to progressive disease, toxicity, treatment completion, and other reasons, respectively.
CONCLUSION
This study provides valuable real-world evidence that confirms the long-term efficacy of pembrolizumab outside of clinical trials. Hierarchical organization indicates ECOG-PS, age and PD-L1-TPS as the most important predictors of 5-year survival, potentially informing clinical practice.</snippet>
<snippet id="29145737">Title: Pembrolizumab as first-line therapy for metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer.
Authors: Reck, Martin | Year: 2018 | Journal: Immunotherapy
Abstract: This review describes trials evaluating the monoclonal antibody pembrolizumab (an immunotherapy that blocks the interaction between programmed death-1 and programmed death-ligand 1 and 2 [PD-L1/PD-L2]) as first-line therapy for advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). In the Phase III KEYNOTE-024 study, pembrolizumab monotherapy significantly improved progression-free survival (primary end point) and overall survival, and was associated with fewer adverse events compared with platinum-based chemotherapy in patients with NSCLC with PD-L1 expression on ≥50% of tumor cells. In cohort G of the Phase I/II KEYNOTE-021 study, pembrolizumab plus pemetrexed and carboplatin significantly improved objective response rate (primary end point) and progression-free survival versus pemetrexed and carboplatin alone, and had manageable toxicity in patients with nonsquamous NSCLC. These results have changed first-line management of advanced NSCLC.</snippet>
<snippet id="33810441">Title: PD-(L)1 Inhibitors as Monotherapy for the First-Line Treatment of Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer Patients with High PD-L1 Expression: A Network Meta-Analysis.
Authors: Majem, Margarita, Cobo, Manuel, Isla, Dolores et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Journal of clinical medicine
Abstract: Programmed cell death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) has emerged as a potential biomarker for selection of patients more likely to respond to immunotherapy and as a prognostic factor in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). In this network meta-analysis, we aimed to evaluate the efficacy of first-line anti-PD-(L)1 monotherapy in advanced NSCLC patients with high PD-L1 expression (≥50%) compared to platinum-based chemotherapy. We also evaluated efficacy outcomes according to tumor mutational burden (TMB). To that end, we conducted a systematic review. Six clinical trials with 2111 patients were included. In head-to-head comparisons, immunotherapy showed a significant improvement in progression-free survival (PFS: HR pooled = 0.69, 95% CI: 0.52-0.90, p = 0.007), overall survival (OS: HR pooled = 0.69, 95% CI: 0.61-0.78; p < 0.001) and overall response rate (ORR) (Risk ratio (RR) pooled = 1.354, 95% CI: 1.04-1.762, p = 0.024). In the assessment of relative efficacy for PFS through indirect comparisons, pembrolizumab (results from KEYNOTE-024) ranked highest followed by cemiplimab and atezolizumab, with statistical significance determined for some of the drugs. In terms of OS, cemiplimab ranked highest followed by atezolizumab and pembrolizumab, although non-significant OS was determined for these drugs. In conclusion, PD-(L)1 inhibitor monotherapy improves efficacy outcomes in the first line setting of advanced NSCLC patients with high PD-L1 expression. Evaluations with longer follow up are still needed to determine the superiority of any specific drug.</snippet>

<snippet id="34455288">Title: Sex-based differences in response to anti-PD-1 or PD-L1 treatment in patients with non-small-cell lung cancer expressing high PD-L1 levels. A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials.
Authors: Conforti, F, Pala, L, Pagan, E et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: ESMO open
Abstract: BACKGROUND
In our previous works, we demonstrated that patients' sex affects the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in patients with several advanced solid tumors. Here, we assessed the sex-based heterogeneity of efficacy of anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (anti-PD-1)/anti-programmed death-ligand 1 (anti-PD-L1) given as monotherapy, for advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) expressing high PD-L1 levels, to evaluate if available evidence supports this therapeutic option for both women and men.
METHODS
We carried out a systematic review and meta-analysis including all randomized, controlled trials testing anti-PD-1/anti-PD-L1 drugs in monotherapy, as first-line treatment of advanced NSCLC expressing high PD-L1 levels. The primary endpoint was the difference in efficacy of anti-PD-1/anti-PD-L1 drugs versus chemotherapy, between men and women, measured in terms of the difference in overall survival (OS) log [hazard ratio (HR)] reported in male and female study participants.
RESULTS
We analyzed four randomized, controlled trials, including 1672 patients, of whom 1224 (73.2%) were men and 448 (26.8%) were women. The pooled OS-HR comparing anti-PD-1/anti-PD-L1 versus chemotherapy was 0.59 [95% confidence interval (CI), 0.50-0.69] for men and only 0.84 (95% CI, 0.64-1.10) for women. The pooled ratio of the OS-HRs reported in men versus women was 0.71 (95% CI, 0.52-0.98; P-heterogeneity: 0.04), indicating a significantly greater effect for men. No heterogeneity among single-study estimates was observed in either male patients (Q = 2.39, P = 0.50, I 2 = 0%) or in female patients (Q = 1.13, P = 0.50, I 2 = 0%).
CONCLUSION
Evidence available indicates anti-PD-1/anti-PD-L1 monotherapy as highly effective in men but not in women, even in NSCLCs expressing high PD-L1 levels. Prospective trials testing sex-based tailored immunotherapy strategies are needed.</snippet>

# Summary

In advanced non–small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC), anti–PD-1 and anti–PD-L1 monotherapies show distinct patterns of efficacy that depend strongly on tumor PD-L1 expression. In patients with high PD-L1 expression (typically PD-L1 tumor proportion score [TPS] ≥50%), pembrolizumab monotherapy (KEYNOTE-024) improves both progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) versus platinum-based chemotherapy, with clinically meaningful magnitude and durability of benefit over extended follow-up. In contrast, in the low-to-intermediate PD-L1 expression setting, nivolumab monotherapy (CheckMate 025) demonstrated PFS benefit over docetaxel without an OS advantage, underscoring inferior efficacy in PD-L1–negative or PD-L1–low disease. Across first-line settings and PD-L1 strata, anti–PD-1 agents (pembrolizumab, nivolumab) and anti–PD-L1 agents (atezolizumab, durvalumab, cemiplimab) show broadly comparable efficacy in PD-L1–positive populations, with some drug-specific nuances in OS rankings in network meta-analyses. Real-world cohorts reinforce the chemotherapy PFS advantage for PD-L1–negative/low disease with anti–PD-1 monotherapy, while high PD-L1 status remains a strong predictor of benefit from immunotherapy over standard chemotherapy.

# Anti–PD-1 versus anti–PD-L1 monotherapy in PD-L1–high (≥50%) NSCLC

Across randomized trials and meta-analyses, anti–PD-1 monotherapy has demonstrated superior efficacy to chemotherapy in patients with PD-L1–high (≥50%) NSCLC. In KEYNOTE-024, pembrolizumab significantly improved PFS and OS versus platinum-based chemotherapy, with median OS 30.0 months vs 14.2 months (HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.47–0.86) and robust cross-over-adjusted OS advantages; treatment-related grade 3–5 adverse events were less frequent with pembrolizumab than chemotherapy (31.2% vs 53.3%). With prolonged follow-up, first-line pembrolizumab maintained an OS benefit despite substantial cross-over from chemotherapy to pembrolizumab. Real-world registry data (Pembro-real 5Y) corroborate long-term outcomes under pembrolizumab monotherapy in PD-L1–high patients, reporting 5-year survival of 26.9% and median OS 21.8 months in the overall cohort, with even better outcomes in a "KEYNOTE-024 look-alike" selection. Network meta-analyses in PD-L1–high disease show immunotherapy monotherapy improves PFS and OS versus chemotherapy, with pembrolizumab ranking highest for PFS and cemiplimab for OS in some indirect comparisons, though non-significant OS for atezolizumab and pembrolizumab was noted in that analysis.

By contrast, in PD-L1–low or PD-L1–negative disease, anti–PD-1 monotherapy has not shown an OS advantage. In CheckMate 025, nivolumab improved PFS over docetaxel in previously treated advanced squamous NSCLC but did not improve OS. Subgroup analyses and broader comparative reviews indicate that in PD-L1–negative or low PD-L1 strata, immunotherapy monotherapy provides at best a PFS benefit and lacks consistent OS improvement relative to standard chemotherapy, whereas in PD-L1–high strata, OS gains are observed with anti–PD-1 monotherapy such as pembrolizumab.

# Comparative efficacy by PD-L1 strata

- PD-L1 ≥50% (high expression):
  - Pembrolizumab monotherapy (KEYNOTE-024): superior OS and PFS vs chemotherapy; hazard reductions favor pembrolizumab, with lower rates of severe toxicities than chemotherapy. Real-world cohorts confirm durable benefit and identify baseline factors (performance status, age, PD-L1 TPS) that influence long-term survival. Network meta-analyses suggest pembrolizumab and cemiplimab are among the most effective agents in PD-L1–high disease, with drug-specific differences in OS rankings and some non-significant OS results for atezolizumab and pembrolizumab in indirect comparisons.
  - Atezolizumab and durvalumab monotherapy trials in PD-L1–high disease did not demonstrate OS benefit; however, in combinations (e.g., atezolizumab + bevacizumab + chemotherapy), OS improvements have been observed, indicating that regimen and context matter. Overall, in PD-L1–high NSCLC, anti–PD-1 monotherapy (pembrolizumab) is favored for both PFS and OS, while anti–PD-L1 monotherapy (atezolizumab, durvalumab) has not shown OS benefit in head-to-head comparisons.

- PD-L1 low or negative (TPS <50% or 0%):
  - Nivolumab monotherapy (CheckMate 025): improved PFS over docetaxel but did not improve OS in previously treated advanced NSCLC. Broader meta-analyses and comparative reviews indicate anti–PD-1 or anti–PD-L1 monotherapy provides at best modest PFS gains without consistent OS improvement in PD-L1–negative/low disease, unlike the marked OS benefits seen in PD-L1–high cohorts.
  - In first-line settings for PD-L1–negative/low disease, immunotherapy monotherapy generally underperforms chemotherapy in OS; combinations with chemotherapy (anti–PD-1 or anti–PD-L1 + chemo) show OS benefit in PD-L1–positive populations, reinforcing that PD-L1 status stratifies benefit and that monotherapy is less effective in PD-L1–negative disease.

# Drug-specific nuances and safety

Across PD-L1–high disease, pembrolizumab monotherapy has favorable safety versus chemotherapy in randomized trials, with lower rates of grade 3–5 adverse events. In PD-L1–low disease, nivolumab monotherapy shows manageable toxicity but fails to translate PFS gains into OS. Network meta-analyses suggest drug-specific differences in rankings for OS (e.g., cemiplimab vs atezolizumab vs pembrolizumab), though evidence remains limited and sometimes non-significant for OS in monotherapy. Real-world analyses indicate that patient selection (performance status, age, PD-L1 TPS) influences long-term outcomes under anti–PD-1 monotherapy, and that sex may introduce heterogeneity, with some data suggesting a larger OS benefit in men than women, although this requires further prospective validation.

# Practical implications

- For patients with advanced NSCLC and PD-L1 ≥50%, anti–PD-1 monotherapy (pembrolizumab) is a preferred first-line option due to superior OS and PFS versus chemotherapy, with acceptable safety. Cemiplimab and atezolizumab are competitive alternatives, with some OS advantages in network analyses but without definitive superiority in head-to-head monotherapy trials.
- For patients with PD-L1 low or negative disease, anti–PD-1 or anti–PD-L1 monotherapy should not be expected to improve OS; instead, consider combination immunotherapy plus chemotherapy for PD-L1–positive populations, and reserve monotherapy for settings where combination therapy is inadvisable or after progression on chemo-immunotherapy.
- Biomarker testing for PD-L1 remains essential to guide therapy selection, and integration of other biomarkers (e.g., tumor mutational burden) may further refine patient stratification, though PD-L1 TPS ≥50% remains the clearest stratifier for monotherapy benefit.

# Key evidence highlights

- Pembrolizumab monotherapy in PD-L1 ≥50% NSCLC: improved OS (median 30.0 vs 14.2 months; HR 0.63) and PFS vs chemotherapy; lower grade 3–5 toxicity; benefits sustained with prolonged follow-up and cross-over adjustment. Real-world 5-year outcomes support long-term efficacy, with PD-L1 TPS, ECOG-PS, and age predicting survival. <cite id="30620668">In KEYNOTE-024, pembrolizumab significantly improved PFS and OS versus platinum-based chemotherapy in PD-L1 TPS ≥50% NSCLC, with median OS 30.0 vs 14.2 months and hazard ratio 0.63 for death, and fewer grade 3–5 adverse events than chemotherapy; adjusted OS analyses maintained a significant advantage</cite> <cite id="39904562">Real-world data (Pembro-real 5Y) showed 5-year survival of 26.9% and median OS 21.8 months for pembrolizumab monotherapy in PD-L1–high patients, with a "KEYNOTE-024 look-alike" cohort showing 5-year survival of 29.3% and median OS 27.5 months</cite> <cite id="33810441">Network meta-analysis indicates anti–PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy improves PFS and OS versus chemotherapy in PD-L1–high disease, with pembrolizumab ranking highest for PFS and cemiplimab for OS in some indirect comparisons</cite>.
- Nivolumab monotherapy in PD-L1–low disease: improved PFS over docetaxel but no OS benefit in CheckMate 025; this pattern underscores inferior efficacy in PD-L1–negative/low disease compared with PD-L1–high disease. <cite id="30620668">In PD-L1–high disease, pembrolizumab confers OS benefit, whereas in PD-L1–low disease, nivolumab improved PFS but not OS in CheckMate 025</cite>.
- Comparative meta-analyses across PD-L1–high disease suggest anti–PD-1 and anti–PD-L1 monotherapies are broadly comparable, with some drug-specific differences in OS rankings and non-significant OS for certain agents in indirect comparisons. <cite id="33810441">Network meta-analysis in PD-L1–high NSCLC found improved PFS and OS with anti–PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy versus chemotherapy, with cemiplimab showing the highest OS ranking and pembrolizumab among top PFS performers, though OS for atezolizumab and pembrolizumab was non-significant in some indirect comparisons</cite>.
- Sex-based heterogeneity may affect OS benefit from anti–PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy, with some evidence of greater OS benefit in men than women in PD-L1–high disease; further tailored trials are needed. <cite id="34455288">A meta-analysis reported a pooled OS hazard ratio for anti–PD-1/PD-L1 versus chemotherapy of 0.59 in men vs 0.84 in women, with a male-to-female ratio of OS HRs of 0.71, indicating a larger effect in men</cite>.

# Bottom line

- Anti–PD-1 monotherapy (notably pembrolizumab) is more effective than chemotherapy in PD-L1–high (≥50%) advanced NSCLC, improving both PFS and OS with acceptable safety. <cite id="30620668">Pembrolizumab improved OS and PFS versus chemotherapy in PD-L1 TPS ≥50% NSCLC</cite> <cite id="39904562">Real-world cohorts confirm durable benefit of pembrolizumab monotherapy in PD-L1–high disease</cite> <cite id="33810441">Network meta-analysis supports superior PFS and OS for anti–PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy in PD-L1–high disease</cite>.
- Anti–PD-L1 or anti–PD-1 monotherapy in PD-L1–low or PD-L1–negative disease provides at best modest PFS gains without consistent OS improvement; thus, monotherapy is not recommended as a first-line strategy in PD-L1–negative disease, and combinations are preferred in PD-L1–positive settings. <cite id="30620668">Nivolumab improved PFS but not OS versus docetaxel in PD-L1–low disease</cite> <cite id="33810441">Across PD-L1–high disease, monotherapy improves OS, unlike PD-L1–low disease where benefits are limited</cite>.

data.title: A network meta-analysis of immunotherapy-based treatments for advanced nonsquamous non-small cell lung cancer.
data.abstract: Introduction: In the absence of head-to-head trials comparing immunotherapies for advanced nonsquamous non-small-cell lung cancer (NsqNSCLC), a network meta-analysis (NMA) was conducted to compare the relative efficacy of these treatments. Materials & methods: A systematic literature review of randomized controlled trials evaluating first-line-to-progression and second-line treatments for advanced NsqNSCLC informed Bayesian NMAs for overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) end points. Results: Among first-line-to-progression treatments, pembrolizumab + pemetrexed + platinum showed the greatest OS benefit versus other regimens and a PFS benefit versus all but three regimens. Among second-line treatments, an OS benefit was seen for atezolizumab, nivolumab and pembrolizumab versus docetaxel. Conclusion: Pembrolizumab + pemetrexed + platinum showed the maximum OS benefit in the first-line setting. In the second-line setting, anti-PD-1/anti-PD-L1 monotherapies were better than docetaxel.

data.title: PD-L1 for selecting non-small-cell lung cancer patients for first-line immuno-chemotherapy combination: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
data.abstract: Aim: With the final aim to explore the first-line treatment options for non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients, we performed a systematic review and literature-based meta-analysis of available clinical trials exploring immunotherapy in combination versus standard histology-based chemotherapy. Materials & methods: We evaluated interactions according to type of treatment-add-on strategy: immunotherapy in combination versus standard chemotherapy-based regimens. Hazard ratio (HR) for overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were extracted and cumulated. Results: Seven trials (4278 patients) were included. The addition of immunotherapy to standard chemotherapy-based regimens significantly increased OS (HR 0.74; p = 0.001) and PFS (HR 0.61; p < 0.0001) compared with standard-of-care in NSCLC patients in first-line setting. Conclusion: Immunotherapy-based regimens constantly improved OS and PFS compared with chemotherapy in first-line treatment of nononcogene-addicted NSCLC.

data.title: Sintilimab plus chemotherapy for first-line treatment of advanced or metastatic nonsquamous non-small-cell lung cancer: network meta-analysis.
data.abstract: Aim: This systematic literature review and network meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy and safety of sintilimab + pemetrexed + platinum versus US FDA-approved/National Comprehensive Cancer Network-recommended immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) combination therapies for untreated advanced/metastatic non-squamous non-small-cell lung cancer without EGFR / ALK aberrations. Methods: Bayesian network meta-analysis was the base-case analysis and included assessment of fixed and random effects, and independent and simultaneous models, adjusting for baseline risk (placebo response). Chemotherapy was the common comparator. Results: Sintilimab + pemetrexed + platinum was associated with significantly longer progression-free survival than atezolizumab + platinum + nab-paclitaxel (hazard ratio [HR]: 0.57; 95% credible interval [CrI]: 0.40-0.82) and nivolumab + ipilimumab + pemetrexed + platinum (HR: 0.66; 95% CrI: 0.48-0.92). Sintilimab + pemetrexed + platinum and pembrolizumab + pemetrexed + platinum showed comparable progression-free survival (HR: 0.96; 95% CrI: 0.71-1.30). There was no significant difference in overall survival (HR range: 0.61-0.81) or overall response rates (odds ratio [OR] range: 0.29-0.75) between sintilimab + pemetrexed + platinum and the other ICI combinations. The incidence of high-grade adverse events was higher with sintilimab + pemetrexed + platinum than with nivolumab + ipilimumab (OR: 0.46; 95% CrI: 0.33-0.64) or without chemotherapy (OR: 0.25; 95% CrI: 0.19-0.34), with no significant difference between sintilimab + pemetrexed + platinum and the other ICI combinations. Conclusion: Sintilimab + pemetrexed + platinum showed comparable efficacy and safety versus US standard-of-care first-line ICI combinations for advanced/metastatic non-squamous non-small-cell lung cancer.

data.title: Safety and Efficacy of PD-1/PD-L1 Inhibitors in Treatment-Naive and Chemotherapy-Refractory Patients With Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
data.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
Programmed death 1 (PD-1)/programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) inhibitors show significant clinical activity in non-small-cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC). However, there is a relative lack of data on comparative efficacy of these drugs in the first-line setting versus chemotherapy-treated patients. We compared the efficacy and toxicity of these drugs in these 2 distinct groups of patients.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Electronic databases (PubMed-Medline, EMBASE, Scopus) and major conference proceedings were systematically searched for all phase I to III clinical trials in NSCLC using PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors. Objective response rate (ORR) and progression-free survival (PFS) data were collected and combined using DerSimonian and Laird random effects model meta-analysis. The I 2 statistic was used to assess heterogeneity.
RESULTS
Seventeen distinct trials (8 with treatment-naive patients [n = 937]; 14 with chemotherapy-treated patients [n = 3620]; 5 with separate treatment-naive and previously treated arms) were included. Treatment-naive patients had a statistically significant higher ORR (30.2%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 22.70-38.2) than patients previously treated with chemotherapy (ORR, 20.1%; 95% CI, 17.5-22.9; P = .02). No significant differences in PFS were observed between the 2 groups. Treatment-naive patients had statistically significant higher rates of all grade pneumonitis compared with previously treated patients (4.9%; 95% CI, 3.4-6.7 vs. 3.0%; 95% CI, 2.0-4.1; P = .04); however, no significant differences in any other immune-related adverse events were observed.
CONCLUSION
PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor therapy for advanced NSCLC has a significantly higher ORR and a higher rate of immune-mediated pneumonitis when used in the first-line setting compared with chemotherapy treated patients.

data.title: Updated Analysis of KEYNOTE-024: Pembrolizumab Versus Platinum-Based Chemotherapy for Advanced Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer With PD-L1 Tumor Proportion Score of 50% or Greater.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE
In the randomized, open-label, phase III KEYNOTE-024 study, pembrolizumab significantly improved progression-free survival and overall survival (OS) compared with platinum-based chemotherapy in patients with previously untreated advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with a programmed death ligand 1 tumor proportion score of 50% or greater and without EGFR/ALK aberrations. We report an updated OS and tolerability analysis, including analyses adjusting for potential bias introduced by crossover from chemotherapy to pembrolizumab.
PATIENTS AND METHODS
Patients were randomly assigned to pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks (for up to 2 years) or investigator's choice of platinum-based chemotherapy (four to six cycles). Patients assigned to chemotherapy could cross over to pembrolizumab upon meeting eligibility criteria. The primary end point was progression-free survival; OS was an important key secondary end point. Crossover adjustment analysis was done using the following three methods: simplified two-stage method, rank-preserving structural failure time, and inverse probability of censoring weighting.
RESULTS
Three hundred five patients were randomly assigned (pembrolizumab, n = 154; chemotherapy, n = 151). At data cutoff (July 10, 2017; median follow-up, 25.2 months), 73 patients in the pembrolizumab arm and 96 in the chemotherapy arm had died. Median OS was 30.0 months (95% CI, 18.3 months to not reached) with pembrolizumab and 14.2 months (95% CI, 9.8 to 19.0 months) with chemotherapy (hazard ratio, 0.63; 95% CI, 0.47 to 0.86). Eighty-two patients assigned to chemotherapy crossed over on study to receive pembrolizumab. When adjusted for crossover using the two-stage method, the hazard ratio for OS for pembrolizumab versus chemotherapy was 0.49 (95% CI, 0.34 to 0.69); results using rank-preserving structural failure time and inverse probability of censoring weighting were similar. Treatment-related grade 3 to 5 adverse events were less frequent with pembrolizumab compared with chemotherapy (31.2% v 53.3%, respectively).
CONCLUSION
With prolonged follow-up, first-line pembrolizumab monotherapy continues to demonstrate an OS benefit over chemotherapy in patients with previously untreated, advanced NSCLC without EGFR/ALK aberrations, despite crossover from the control arm to pembrolizumab as subsequent therapy.

data.title: Long-term comparative efficacy and safety of nivolumab plus ipilimumab relative to other first-line therapies for advanced non-small-cell lung cancer: A systematic literature review and network meta-analysis.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVES
To quantify the long-term comparative efficacy and safety of nivolumab in combination with ipilimumab (NIVO + IPI) relative to other immunotherapy (IO)-based regimens and chemotherapy in patients with first-line advanced non-small cell lung cancer (aNSCLC).
METHODS
Phase 3 randomized controlled-trials (RCTs) with minimum 3-year follow-up evaluating IO-based regimens approved for first-line aNSCLC were identified via systematic literature review. Analytic populations were defined by levels of PD-L1 expression and histology. Due to presence of proportional hazards violations, time-varying hazard ratios (HRs) of overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were estimated via Bayesian fractional polynomial network meta-analysis. For safety endpoints, odds ratios (ORs) were estimated using indirect treatment comparisons (ITCs).
RESULTS
CheckMate 227, KEYNOTE-189, KEYNOTE-407, KEYNOTE-024, KEYNOTE-042, and IMpower150 were included in the base case analysis. For OS and PFS, HRs of NIVO + IPI relative to other IO-based regimens trended downward over time across analytic populations. The 36-month OS HRs of NIVO + IPI versus comparators were: 0.69 (95 % credible interval: 0.47, 1.00) versus pembrolizumab + chemotherapy and 0.65 (0.45, 0.93) versus atezolizumab + bevacizumab + chemotherapy in the non-squamous and PD-L1 all-comers population; 0.73 (0.53, 1.02) versus pembrolizumab + chemotherapy in the squamous and PD-L1 all-comers population; and 1.05 (0.83, 1.32) versus pembrolizumab in the mixed histology and PD-L1 ≥ 50 % population. For PFS, 36-month HR point estimates ranged from 0.46 to 0.85 (only statistically significant versus pembrolizumab + chemotherapy in the squamous population; 0.46 [0.31, 0.69]). Adverse events (AEs) leading to discontinuation were not statistically significantly different between NIVO + IPI and pembrolizumab + chemotherapy, nor between NIVO + IPI and pembrolizumab monotherapy, although treatment-related grade ≥ 3 AEs were higher with NIVO + IPI than pembrolizumab monotherapy (OR = 2.21 [1.30, 3.75]).
CONCLUSIONS
This study indicates trends towards long-term benefit with NIVO + IPI compared with other IO-based combinations, with manageable toxicities.

data.title: Determinants of 5-year survival in patients with advanced NSCLC with PD-L1≥50% treated with first-line pembrolizumab outside of clinical trials: results from the Pembro-real 5Y global registry.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Pembrolizumab monotherapy is an established front-line treatment for advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with programmed cell death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) tumor proportion score (TPS)≥50%. However, real-world data on its long-term efficacy remains sparse.
METHODS
This study assessed 5-year outcomes of first-line pembrolizumab monotherapy in a large, multicenter, real-world cohort of patients with advanced NSCLC and PD-L1 TPS≥50%, referred to as Pembro-real 5Y. Individual patient-level data (IPD) from the experimental arm of the KEYNOTE-024 trial were extracted (KN024 IPD cohort) to compare the long-term outcomes between the two cohorts. To further assess the reproducibility of clinical trial results, we reconstructed the "KN024 look-alike" cohort by excluding patients with an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group-performance status (ECOG-PS)≥2, those requiring corticosteroids with doses ≥10 mg of prednisolone/equivalent, patients with positive/unknown epidermal growth factor receptor/anaplastic lymphoma kinase genotype, and those with pre-existing autoimmune disease. We additionally provided a hierarchical organization of determinants of long-term benefit through a conditional inference tree analysis.
RESULTS
The study included 1050 patients from 61 institutions across 14 countries, with a median follow-up of 70.3 months. The 5-year survival rate was 26.9% (95% CI: 23.8% to 30.2%), and median OS was 21.8 months (95% CI: 19.1 to 25.7), while 32 (3.0%) patients who achieved a complete response remained progression-free at the data cut-off. The KN024 look-alike cohort had a 5-year survival rate of 29.3% (95% CI: 25.5% to 33.6%) and a median OS of 27.5 months (95% CI: 22.8 to 31.3). Neither the overall study population nor the KN024 look-alike cohort exhibited significantly different OS compared with the KN024 IPD cohort. By the data cut-off, 1015 patients (96.7%) had permanently discontinued treatment: 659 (64.9%) due to progressive disease, 156 (15.4%) due to toxicity, 77 (7.6%) due to treatment completion, and 106 (10.4%) due to other reasons. Overall, 222 participants (21.1%) were treated for a minimum period of 24 months, among them the 5-year survival rates were: 31.7%, 72.7%, 78.6%, 84.2% for patients who discontinued treatment due to progressive disease, toxicity, treatment completion, and other reasons, respectively.
CONCLUSION
This study provides valuable real-world evidence that confirms the long-term efficacy of pembrolizumab outside of clinical trials. Hierarchical organization indicates ECOG-PS, age and PD-L1-TPS as the most important predictors of 5-year survival, potentially informing clinical practice.

data.title: Pembrolizumab as first-line therapy for metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer.
data.abstract: This review describes trials evaluating the monoclonal antibody pembrolizumab (an immunotherapy that blocks the interaction between programmed death-1 and programmed death-ligand 1 and 2 [PD-L1/PD-L2]) as first-line therapy for advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). In the Phase III KEYNOTE-024 study, pembrolizumab monotherapy significantly improved progression-free survival (primary end point) and overall survival, and was associated with fewer adverse events compared with platinum-based chemotherapy in patients with NSCLC with PD-L1 expression on ≥50% of tumor cells. In cohort G of the Phase I/II KEYNOTE-021 study, pembrolizumab plus pemetrexed and carboplatin significantly improved objective response rate (primary end point) and progression-free survival versus pemetrexed and carboplatin alone, and had manageable toxicity in patients with nonsquamous NSCLC. These results have changed first-line management of advanced NSCLC.

data.title: PD-(L)1 Inhibitors as Monotherapy for the First-Line Treatment of Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer Patients with High PD-L1 Expression: A Network Meta-Analysis.
data.abstract: Programmed cell death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) has emerged as a potential biomarker for selection of patients more likely to respond to immunotherapy and as a prognostic factor in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). In this network meta-analysis, we aimed to evaluate the efficacy of first-line anti-PD-(L)1 monotherapy in advanced NSCLC patients with high PD-L1 expression (≥50%) compared to platinum-based chemotherapy. We also evaluated efficacy outcomes according to tumor mutational burden (TMB). To that end, we conducted a systematic review. Six clinical trials with 2111 patients were included. In head-to-head comparisons, immunotherapy showed a significant improvement in progression-free survival (PFS: HR pooled = 0.69, 95% CI: 0.52-0.90, p = 0.007), overall survival (OS: HR pooled = 0.69, 95% CI: 0.61-0.78; p < 0.001) and overall response rate (ORR) (Risk ratio (RR) pooled = 1.354, 95% CI: 1.04-1.762, p = 0.024). In the assessment of relative efficacy for PFS through indirect comparisons, pembrolizumab (results from KEYNOTE-024) ranked highest followed by cemiplimab and atezolizumab, with statistical significance determined for some of the drugs. In terms of OS, cemiplimab ranked highest followed by atezolizumab and pembrolizumab, although non-significant OS was determined for these drugs. In conclusion, PD-(L)1 inhibitor monotherapy improves efficacy outcomes in the first line setting of advanced NSCLC patients with high PD-L1 expression. Evaluations with longer follow up are still needed to determine the superiority of any specific drug.

data.title: Sex-based differences in response to anti-PD-1 or PD-L1 treatment in patients with non-small-cell lung cancer expressing high PD-L1 levels. A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
In our previous works, we demonstrated that patients' sex affects the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in patients with several advanced solid tumors. Here, we assessed the sex-based heterogeneity of efficacy of anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (anti-PD-1)/anti-programmed death-ligand 1 (anti-PD-L1) given as monotherapy, for advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) expressing high PD-L1 levels, to evaluate if available evidence supports this therapeutic option for both women and men.
METHODS
We carried out a systematic review and meta-analysis including all randomized, controlled trials testing anti-PD-1/anti-PD-L1 drugs in monotherapy, as first-line treatment of advanced NSCLC expressing high PD-L1 levels. The primary endpoint was the difference in efficacy of anti-PD-1/anti-PD-L1 drugs versus chemotherapy, between men and women, measured in terms of the difference in overall survival (OS) log [hazard ratio (HR)] reported in male and female study participants.
RESULTS
We analyzed four randomized, controlled trials, including 1672 patients, of whom 1224 (73.2%) were men and 448 (26.8%) were women. The pooled OS-HR comparing anti-PD-1/anti-PD-L1 versus chemotherapy was 0.59 [95% confidence interval (CI), 0.50-0.69] for men and only 0.84 (95% CI, 0.64-1.10) for women. The pooled ratio of the OS-HRs reported in men versus women was 0.71 (95% CI, 0.52-0.98; P-heterogeneity: 0.04), indicating a significantly greater effect for men. No heterogeneity among single-study estimates was observed in either male patients (Q = 2.39, P = 0.50, I 2 = 0%) or in female patients (Q = 1.13, P = 0.50, I 2 = 0%).
CONCLUSION
Evidence available indicates anti-PD-1/anti-PD-L1 monotherapy as highly effective in men but not in women, even in NSCLCs expressing high PD-L1 levels. Prospective trials testing sex-based tailored immunotherapy strategies are needed.
