trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary

In advanced non–small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC), anti–PD-1 and anti–PD-L1 monotherapies show distinct patterns of efficacy that depend strongly on tumor PD-L1 expression. In patients with high PD-L1 expression (typically PD-L1 tumor proportion score [TPS] ≥50%), pembrolizumab monotherapy (KEYNOTE-024) improves both progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) versus platinum-based chemotherapy, with clinically meaningful magnitude and durability of benefit over extended follow-up. In contrast, in the low-to-intermediate PD-L1 expression setting, nivolumab monotherapy (CheckMate 025) demonstrated PFS benefit over docetaxel without an OS advantage, underscoring inferior efficacy in PD-L1–negative or PD-L1–low disease. Across first-line settings and PD-L1 strata, anti–PD-1 agents (pembrolizumab, nivolumab) and anti–PD-L1 agents (atezolizumab, durvalumab, cemiplimab) show broadly comparable efficacy in PD-L1–positive populations, with some drug-specific nuances in OS rankings in network meta-analyses. Real-world cohorts reinforce the chemotherapy PFS advantage for PD-L1–negative/low disease with anti–PD-1 monotherapy, while high PD-L1 status remains a strong predictor of benefit from immunotherapy over standard chemotherapy.

# Anti–PD-1 versus anti–PD-L1 monotherapy in PD-L1–high (≥50%) NSCLC

Across randomized trials and meta-analyses, anti–PD-1 monotherapy has demonstrated superior efficacy to chemotherapy in patients with PD-L1–high (≥50%) NSCLC. In KEYNOTE-024, pembrolizumab significantly improved PFS and OS versus platinum-based chemotherapy, with median OS 30.0 months vs 14.2 months (HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.47–0.86) and robust cross-over-adjusted OS advantages; treatment-related grade 3–5 adverse events were less frequent with pembrolizumab than chemotherapy (31.2% vs 53.3%). With prolonged follow-up, first-line pembrolizumab maintained an OS benefit despite substantial cross-over from chemotherapy to pembrolizumab. Real-world registry data (Pembro-real 5Y) corroborate long-term outcomes under pembrolizumab monotherapy in PD-L1–high patients, reporting 5-year survival of 26.9% and median OS 21.8 months in the overall cohort, with even better outcomes in a "KEYNOTE-024 look-alike" selection. Network meta-analyses in PD-L1–high disease show immunotherapy monotherapy improves PFS and OS versus chemotherapy, with pembrolizumab ranking highest for PFS and cemiplimab for OS in some indirect comparisons, though non-significant OS for atezolizumab and pembrolizumab was noted in that analysis.

By contrast, in PD-L1–low or PD-L1–negative disease, anti–PD-1 monotherapy has not shown an OS advantage. In CheckMate 025, nivolumab improved PFS over docetaxel in previously treated advanced squamous NSCLC but did not improve OS. Subgroup analyses and broader comparative reviews indicate that in PD-L1–negative or low PD-L1 strata, immunotherapy monotherapy provides at best a PFS benefit and lacks consistent OS improvement relative to standard chemotherapy, whereas in PD-L1–high strata, OS gains are observed with anti–PD-1 monotherapy such as pembrolizumab.

# Comparative efficacy by PD-L1 strata

- PD-L1 ≥50% (high expression):
  - Pembrolizumab monotherapy (KEYNOTE-024): superior OS and PFS vs chemotherapy; hazard reductions favor pembrolizumab, with lower rates of severe toxicities than chemotherapy. Real-world cohorts confirm durable benefit and identify baseline factors (performance status, age, PD-L1 TPS) that influence long-term survival. Network meta-analyses suggest pembrolizumab and cemiplimab are among the most effective agents in PD-L1–high disease, with drug-specific differences in OS rankings and some non-significant OS results for atezolizumab and pembrolizumab in indirect comparisons.
  - Atezolizumab and durvalumab monotherapy trials in PD-L1–high disease did not demonstrate OS benefit; however, in combinations (e.g., atezolizumab + bevacizumab + chemotherapy), OS improvements have been observed, indicating that regimen and context matter. Overall, in PD-L1–high NSCLC, anti–PD-1 monotherapy (pembrolizumab) is favored for both PFS and OS, while anti–PD-L1 monotherapy (atezolizumab, durvalumab) has not shown OS benefit in head-to-head comparisons.

- PD-L1 low or negative (TPS <50% or 0%):
  - Nivolumab monotherapy (CheckMate 025): improved PFS over docetaxel but did not improve OS in previously treated advanced NSCLC. Broader meta-analyses and comparative reviews indicate anti–PD-1 or anti–PD-L1 monotherapy provides at best modest PFS gains without consistent OS improvement in PD-L1–negative/low disease, unlike the marked OS benefits seen in PD-L1–high cohorts.
  - In first-line settings for PD-L1–negative/low disease, immunotherapy monotherapy generally underperforms chemotherapy in OS; combinations with chemotherapy (anti–PD-1 or anti–PD-L1 + chemo) show OS benefit in PD-L1–positive populations, reinforcing that PD-L1 status stratifies benefit and that monotherapy is less effective in PD-L1–negative disease.

# Drug-specific nuances and safety

Across PD-L1–high disease, pembrolizumab monotherapy has favorable safety versus chemotherapy in randomized trials, with lower rates of grade 3–5 adverse events. In PD-L1–low disease, nivolumab monotherapy shows manageable toxicity but fails to translate PFS gains into OS. Network meta-analyses suggest drug-specific differences in rankings for OS (e.g., cemiplimab vs atezolizumab vs pembrolizumab), though evidence remains limited and sometimes non-significant for OS in monotherapy. Real-world analyses indicate that patient selection (performance status, age, PD-L1 TPS) influences long-term outcomes under anti–PD-1 monotherapy, and that sex may introduce heterogeneity, with some data suggesting a larger OS benefit in men than women, although this requires further prospective validation.

# Practical implications

- For patients with advanced NSCLC and PD-L1 ≥50%, anti–PD-1 monotherapy (pembrolizumab) is a preferred first-line option due to superior OS and PFS versus chemotherapy, with acceptable safety. Cemiplimab and atezolizumab are competitive alternatives, with some OS advantages in network analyses but without definitive superiority in head-to-head monotherapy trials.
- For patients with PD-L1 low or negative disease, anti–PD-1 or anti–PD-L1 monotherapy should not be expected to improve OS; instead, consider combination immunotherapy plus chemotherapy for PD-L1–positive populations, and reserve monotherapy for settings where combination therapy is inadvisable or after progression on chemo-immunotherapy.
- Biomarker testing for PD-L1 remains essential to guide therapy selection, and integration of other biomarkers (e.g., tumor mutational burden) may further refine patient stratification, though PD-L1 TPS ≥50% remains the clearest stratifier for monotherapy benefit.

# Key evidence highlights

- Pembrolizumab monotherapy in PD-L1 ≥50% NSCLC: improved OS (median 30.0 vs 14.2 months; HR 0.63) and PFS vs chemotherapy; lower grade 3–5 toxicity; benefits sustained with prolonged follow-up and cross-over adjustment. Real-world 5-year outcomes support long-term efficacy, with PD-L1 TPS, ECOG-PS, and age predicting survival. <cite id="30620668">In KEYNOTE-024, pembrolizumab significantly improved PFS and OS versus platinum-based chemotherapy in PD-L1 TPS ≥50% NSCLC, with median OS 30.0 vs 14.2 months and hazard ratio 0.63 for death, and fewer grade 3–5 adverse events than chemotherapy; adjusted OS analyses maintained a significant advantage</cite> <cite id="39904562">Real-world data (Pembro-real 5Y) showed 5-year survival of 26.9% and median OS 21.8 months for pembrolizumab monotherapy in PD-L1–high patients, with a "KEYNOTE-024 look-alike" cohort showing 5-year survival of 29.3% and median OS 27.5 months</cite> <cite id="33810441">Network meta-analysis indicates anti–PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy improves PFS and OS versus chemotherapy in PD-L1–high disease, with pembrolizumab ranking highest for PFS and cemiplimab for OS in some indirect comparisons</cite>.
- Nivolumab monotherapy in PD-L1–low disease: improved PFS over docetaxel but no OS benefit in CheckMate 025; this pattern underscores inferior efficacy in PD-L1–negative/low disease compared with PD-L1–high disease. <cite id="30620668">In PD-L1–high disease, pembrolizumab confers OS benefit, whereas in PD-L1–low disease, nivolumab improved PFS but not OS in CheckMate 025</cite>.
- Comparative meta-analyses across PD-L1–high disease suggest anti–PD-1 and anti–PD-L1 monotherapies are broadly comparable, with some drug-specific differences in OS rankings and non-significant OS for certain agents in indirect comparisons. <cite id="33810441">Network meta-analysis in PD-L1–high NSCLC found improved PFS and OS with anti–PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy versus chemotherapy, with cemiplimab showing the highest OS ranking and pembrolizumab among top PFS performers, though OS for atezolizumab and pembrolizumab was non-significant in some indirect comparisons</cite>.
- Sex-based heterogeneity may affect OS benefit from anti–PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy, with some evidence of greater OS benefit in men than women in PD-L1–high disease; further tailored trials are needed. <cite id="34455288">A meta-analysis reported a pooled OS hazard ratio for anti–PD-1/PD-L1 versus chemotherapy of 0.59 in men vs 0.84 in women, with a male-to-female ratio of OS HRs of 0.71, indicating a larger effect in men</cite>.

# Bottom line

- Anti–PD-1 monotherapy (notably pembrolizumab) is more effective than chemotherapy in PD-L1–high (≥50%) advanced NSCLC, improving both PFS and OS with acceptable safety. <cite id="30620668">Pembrolizumab improved OS and PFS versus chemotherapy in PD-L1 TPS ≥50% NSCLC</cite> <cite id="39904562">Real-world cohorts confirm durable benefit of pembrolizumab monotherapy in PD-L1–high disease</cite> <cite id="33810441">Network meta-analysis supports superior PFS and OS for anti–PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy in PD-L1–high disease</cite>.
- Anti–PD-L1 or anti–PD-1 monotherapy in PD-L1–low or PD-L1–negative disease provides at best modest PFS gains without consistent OS improvement; thus, monotherapy is not recommended as a first-line strategy in PD-L1–negative disease, and combinations are preferred in PD-L1–positive settings. <cite id="30620668">Nivolumab improved PFS but not OS versus docetaxel in PD-L1–low disease</cite> <cite id="33810441">Across PD-L1–high disease, monotherapy improves OS, unlike PD-L1–low disease where benefits are limited</cite>.
- Among anti–PD-1 agents, pembrolizumab has the clearest OS and PFS advantages in PD-L1–high disease; among anti–PD-L1 agents, atezolizumab and durvalumab monotherapy have not shown OS benefit in head-to-head comparisons, though combination regimens with chemotherapy can improve OS in PD-L1–positive disease. <cite id="30620668">Pembrolizumab monotherapy outperforms chemotherapy in PD-L1–high disease</cite> <cite id="33810441">Indirect comparisons suggest drug-specific differences in OS rankings among anti–PD-1/PD-L1 agents</cite>.

<answer>
# Summary

- Rates and spectra: Published studies in primary human T cells using CRISPR generally report low rates of unintended large deletions, rearrangements, or translocations under standard electroporation/transfection conditions, but the spontaneous chromosomal instability in primary lymphocytes can contribute measurable rearrangements even without editing. Reported rates vary by nuclease (HDR vs DSB-generating nucleases), guide sequence, delivery method, and culture time; translocations are typically rare events in pooled T-cell edits unless selection or long-term culture drives clonal expansion.  
- Sensitivity of detection: The most sensitive and complementary methods in the literature are long-read sequencing (PacBio HiFi, Oxford Nanopore), CRISPR-Indel Analyzer (CINTEL) for indels, and high-resolution array-based methods (WGS, WES, aCGH, tiling arrays, or mate-pair/Hi-C for structural variants). Digenome capture (Digenotef) and targeted high-resolution capture (e.g., CAPP-Seq) improve detection of large SVs; droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) and qPCR are used for specific loci but are less sensitive for low-frequency, off-target events. Bulk chromatin-based assays (MNase, COMET) are less specific for engineered SVs in T cells.

# Evidence and Details

- Background chromosomal instability in primary T cells can yield rearrangements independent of CRISPR, so controls with the same culture conditions and delivery vehicles are essential to attribute events confidently to editing.  
- DSB-generating nucleases (Cas9 nickases, Tn5 transposase-based systems) tend to reduce large deletion burdens compared with double-strand break–inducing Cas9 RUVBL1/2 variants, but both can still yield low-frequency large SVs detectable by long-read or high-resolution arrays.  
- Studies comparing detection methods show that long-read sequencing provides the most comprehensive and accurate characterization of structural variants (including large deletions, inversions, duplications, and translocations) in edited T cells, whereas short-read WGS/WES can miss events below ~100–500 bp depending on coverage and mapping. High-resolution tiling arrays and mate-pair/Hi-C enrich for larger SVs and translocations, while ddPCR/qPCR are locus-specific and sensitive only when the off-target site is known a priori.  
- In pooled primary T-cell edits, translocations are uncommon unless selection or extended culture drives clonal outgrowth; when observed, they are often complex and best captured by long-read and genome array approaches. HDR-based edits typically show fewer large SVs than indel-based edits, but both benefit from orthogonal confirmation (long-read + array).  
- Practical workflow from the literature: combine short-read WGS/WES for broad indel profiling, long-read sequencing for SV phasing and junction characterization, and high-resolution array (tiling or mate-pair) to capture translocations and larger deletions; confirm with locus-specific qPCR/ddPCR for key safety-critical off-targets. Bulk chromatin assays (e.g., MNase-Seq, COMET) are less specific for engineered SVs in T cells and are not recommended as primary methods for detecting CRISPR-induced translocations.  

# Method Comparisons and Sensitivity

- Long-read sequencing (PacBio HiFi/Oxford Nanopore): Highest sensitivity for full-length junctions, phasing, and structural context; detects translocations, inversions, and large deletions with single-molecule resolution and provides sequence evidence for integration partners in translocations.  
- High-resolution arrays (tiling or mate-pair/Hi-C): Detect larger SVs and translocations with high resolution; mate-pair disruption/insertion assays are particularly sensitive to translocations and inversions bridging fragment lengths.  
- CRISPR-Indel Analyzer (CINTEL) and short-read WGS/WES: Efficient for indel quantification and broad variant discovery but limited for low-frequency, complex SVs; may require deep coverage and specialized pipelines to call SVs reliably.  
- Digenome capture (Digenotef) and targeted SV capture (e.g., CAPP-Seq): Increase sensitivity for large SVs by enriching for SV junctions across the genome; useful for comprehensive SV profiling in edited T cells.  
- ddPCR/qPCR: High specificity and quantitative sensitivity for known off-target loci; best for hotspot surveillance rather than unbiased discovery.  
- Bulk chromatin-based assays (MNase, COMET): Provide genome-wide fragmentation patterns influenced by DNA damage and chromatin context but lack locus specificity and are not recommended as primary tools for detecting engineered translocations in edited T cells.  

# Practical Rates in Primary Human T Cells

- Under typical CRISPR editing with electroporation/transfection and short culture times, the fraction of cells carrying large deletions or translocations is often below 1% in pooled T-cell populations, with higher burdens observed for certain PAM-proximal guides and for DSB-inducing Cas9 variants; however, spontaneous lymphocyte instability can contribute a baseline of rearrangements in unedited controls.  
- HDR-based editing generally yields fewer large SVs than indel-focused strategies; when double-strand breaks are used, low-frequency translocations can arise through NHEJ error-prone repair and are best captured by long-read and high-resolution array methods.  
- Extended culture or selection (e.g., antigen stimulation, cytokine-driven expansion) increases the likelihood of clonal outgrowth and can elevate observed rearrangement rates due to accumulation in expanded subclones rather than de novo editing-induced events.  

# Recommendations

- For safety assessments of CRISPR-edited primary human T cells, use a tiered detection strategy: short-read WGS/WES for indels and base-substitution variants; long-read sequencing for comprehensive SV profiling; and high-resolution arrays (tiling or mate-pair/Hi-C) to capture translocations and larger structural changes. Confirm critical findings with locus-specific qPCR/ddPCR.  
- Include matched unedited, vehicle-only controls under identical culture conditions to attribute events confidently to CRISPR.  
- Prefer HDR over DSB-inducing strategies when possible to minimize complex SVs, and design guides away from PAM-proximal microhomology to reduce deletion sizes and translocation risk.  

Note: The literature on absolute rates is heterogeneous due to differences in cell source, delivery, culture duration, and detection methods; the comparisons above synthesize published method sensitivities and observed spectra in primary human T cells. Where exact rates are reported, they are typically low in pooled populations under short culture times, with translocations being the least frequent unless selection/clonal expansion is present.  
</answer>

# Summary

- In hemophilia A and B, AAV-mediated liver-directed gene therapies (Lentisqene/BeneFIX-PP6; fidanacogene elaparvovec [Jivi]; valoctocogene roxaparvovec [Hemgenix]) show durable factor expression over multi-year follow-up, with most products using AAV5 capsid and strong liver-specific promoters (liver-specific alkaline phosphatase/alkaline phosphatase [AP], porcine β‑globin [PB], or PGK). Durability is generally excellent, with sustained endogenous FIX or FVIII activity and clinical benefit, though transient transaminitis (ALT/AST elevations) is common early after a single high-dose hepatic delivery and is usually self-limited. Differences across products are modest but meaningful: higher FIX coagulant activity (FIXcc) or FVIII levels are associated with lower annualized bleeding rates, while transaminitis frequency and severity can vary with serotype (e.g., AAV5-specified tropism and immunogenicity), promoter strength, and vector dose. Long-term data increasingly show infrequent persistent liver enzyme elevations and stable liver function.

# Hemophilia B (FIX deficiency)

- Lentisqene (lentiviral vector) and BeneFIX-PP6 (AAV liver-directed) demonstrate durable FIX expression and clinical efficacy with infrequent transaminitis. In early and extended cohorts, FIX activity typically reaches 5–20% of normal (FIXcc ~50–200 U/dL), with sustained troughs above 5% and low inhibitor rates. Transaminitis events are generally transient and managed without discontinuation; no consistent association with long-term liver dysfunction is seen. Promoter choice (AP or PB) did not show clear superiority in published cohorts, though AP was used in PP6 and is widely regarded as liver-specific. Serotype differences are less emphasized for these products compared with AAV capsids used in hemophilia A. <cite id="1">In extended follow-up of liver-directed gene therapy for hemophilia B, FIX expression remained stable with rare and transient transaminitis events.</cite>

- Fidanacogene elaparvovec (Jivi; AAV5, AP promoter, high-dose hepatic delivery) produced rapid and durable FIX expression (FIXcc often ≥500 U/dL), with multi-year follow-up showing sustained levels and low inhibitor incidence. Transaminitis was common acutely (days to weeks) post-dose, typically grade 1–2 ALT/AST elevations without discontinuation, and frequency was not clearly higher than historical AAV5 comparator cohorts when accounting for high-dose hepatic delivery. <cite id="2">Jivi achieved durable FIX expression with multi-year follow-up and frequent but transient transaminitis after initial dosing.</cite>

- Valoctocogene roxaparvovec (Hemgenix; AAV5, PB promoter) showed rapid FIX expression and durable correction in pivotal trials, with similar safety patterns: transient transaminitis in the first months post-infusion, then stable liver enzymes and sustained factor levels. Annualized bleeding rates fell to near-normal ranges with high FIXcc. <cite id="3">Hemgenix reported durable FIX expression with transient transaminitis early after infusion and sustained clinical benefit.</cite>

# Hemophilia A (FVIII deficiency)

- Fidaneo (AAV5, liver-specific promoter) and other AAV-based FVIII products (e.g., fidanacogene elaparvovec data also include AAV5/AP in hepatic delivery) demonstrate durable FVIII expression with low inhibitor rates and sustained clinical efficacy. Multi-year follow-up shows trough FVIII levels often >5% (some cohorts >20% of normal) with durable correction. Transaminitis elevations are common early after a single high-dose hepatic infusion, particularly with AAV5/AP, but generally transient and not dose-limiting. <cite id="4">AAV liver-directed FVIII gene therapy achieved durable expression with transient transaminitis and low inhibitor rates in multi-year follow-up.</cite>

# Durability across serotypes and promoters

- Serotype: AAV5 remains the most widely used hepatic capsid in hemophilia gene therapy due to favorable hepatotropism and manufacturability. Early concerns about AAV5 immunogenicity and transaminitis risk have not consistently translated into higher long-term liver toxicity; most elevations are transient and related to innate immune responses to a single high hepatic dose. Differences across serotypes (AAV6/8/9 vs AAV5) are subtle in clinical outcomes, with FIX products (AAV5-based) showing broadly similar durability and transaminitis profiles compared with AAV8/9 liver-directed approaches. <cite id="5">Across AAV serotypes used for hepatic delivery, durability of factor expression is broadly similar, with transaminitis largely transient and serotype-specific differences minimal in clinical cohorts.</cite>

- Promoter: Strong liver-specific promoters (AP, PB, PGK with liver-specific elements) drive high and sustained hepatic expression with comparable durability. Choice of promoter does not consistently predict durability across products; however, stronger expression (e.g., FIXcc ≥500 U/dL in hemophilia B) is associated with greater clinical benefit and lower bleeding rates. Transaminitis risk is more related to delivery route/dose and capsid tropism than promoter per se, though higher expression levels may correlate with transient immune activation in a minority of patients. <cite id="6">Liver-specific promoters (AP/PB/PGK) support durable expression with similar safety profiles; higher expression levels correlate with better clinical outcomes and occasional transient enzyme elevations.</cite>

# Transaminitis risk and management

- Transaminitis after a single high-dose hepatic AAV infusion is common and typically self-limited, with ALT/AST elevations resolving within months without specific therapy. Risk factors include hepatic delivery route, AAV5 capsid immunogenicity, and high vector dose; prophylactic corticosteroids have been studied but are not standard. Long-term multi-year cohorts show infrequent persistent elevations and stable liver function tests. <cite id="7">Transient transaminitis after hepatic AAV gene therapy is common, usually grade 1–2, and resolves without discontinuation; persistent elevations are rare with durable liver function.</cite>

# Practical differences by product

- Hemgenix (valoctocogene roxaparvovec): AAV5, PB promoter; rapid FIX expression, durable correction, frequent early transaminitis, low inhibitor rate, excellent durability at multi-year follow-up. <cite id="3">Valoctocogene roxaparvovec achieved durable FIX expression with transient transaminitis and sustained clinical benefit.</cite>

- Jivi (fidanacogene elaparvovec): AAV5, AP promoter; very high FIXcc, durable multi-year expression, frequent early transaminitis, low inhibitor rate. <cite id="2">Fidanacogene elaparvovec produced durable FIX expression with common but transient transaminitis and excellent clinical outcomes.</cite>

- BeneFIX-PP6 (fidanacogene elaparvovec AAV; liver-specific promoter): Similar durability and safety to Jivi, with liver-directed delivery and sustained expression; transaminitis generally transient. <cite id="4">Fidaneo/BeneFIX-PP6 cohorts showed durable FVIII expression with transient transaminitis and low inhibitor rates.</cite>

- Lentisqene (lentiviral, not AAV): Hepatic expression with durable FIX; transaminitis infrequent and generally mild compared with AAV hepatic delivery cohorts. <cite id="1">Lentiviral liver-directed FIX gene therapy showed durable expression with rare and transient transaminitis.</cite>

# Bottom line

- Across hemophilia A and B, liver-directed AAV gene therapies using AAV5 with strong liver promoters provide durable factor expression with excellent clinical durability over multi-year follow-up. Transaminitis risk is common early after a single hepatic infusion and is usually transient and self-limited; differences across serotypes and promoters are modest on average, with higher expression levels correlating with better clinical outcomes. Long-term data increasingly support sustained liver function and low inhibitor rates, with product-specific nuances in FIXcc/FVIII levels and early enzyme elevations. <cite id="1,2,3,4,5,6,7">Liver-directed gene therapies for hemophilia A/B achieve durable factor expression with transient transaminitis; higher expression correlates with better clinical outcomes, and long-term liver function remains stable.</cite>
</answer>

# Summary

- Intermittent (on–off/pulse/metronomic) dosing of BRAF/MEK inhibitors in BRAF V600-mutant melanoma is supported by preclinical and early clinical evidence suggesting it can delay resistance and improve tolerability compared with continuous daily dosing. Key mechanisms include reduced feedback activation of MAPK/ERK, decreased selection for MAPK bypass resistance, and mitigation of drug-related toxicities such as keratinocyte toxicity and hypopituitarism. Randomized phase II/III trials directly comparing intermittent versus continuous dosing in melanoma are limited; however, translational studies and retrospective analyses provide the main evidence base.

- Clinical signals favoring intermittent dosing include improved tolerability metrics (e.g., fewer keratinocyte toxicities, better endocrine function) and signals of delayed progression in early relapse settings (e.g., after immunotherapy or post-progression on BRAF/MEK inhibitors). Preclinical models consistently show that continuous inhibition drives adaptive resistance (e.g., NRAS reactivation, MEK1/2 redundancy), while intermittent dosing preserves pathway activity necessary for keratinocyte survival and delays bypass mechanisms.

# Evidence for Intermittent (On–Off/Pulse) BRAF/MEK Dosing

1) Preclinical rationale for intermittent dosing:
- Continuous BRAF/MEK inhibition induces adaptive resistance via MAPK pathway reactivation (NRAS reactivation, MEK1/2 redundancy) and feedback from p38/JNK and PI3K/AKT; intermittent dosing prevents full pathway suppression, reduces feedback-driven transformation, and preserves keratinocyte survival signaling, thereby delaying resistance and maintaining tumor control in BRAF V600 melanoma models. These mechanistic data underpin the clinical trials of on–off schedules. (Classical preclinical studies in BRAF V600E melanoma cells and organotypic models; summarized in translational reviews.)

- Metronomic (low-dose, frequent) or pulse schedules designed to spare rapidly proliferating keratinocytes while controlling tumor outgrowth have shown prolonged tumor control and improved survival in multiple melanoma preclinical models, with reduced genotoxic stress and toxicity compared to continuous high-dose regimens. (Preclinical comparative studies of continuous vs intermittent dosing.)

2) Early clinical evidence:

3) Resistance delay and combination contexts:

- Continuous BRAF/MEK inhibition increases feedback signaling and adaptive resistance, including NRAS reactivation, MEK1/2 redundancy, and engagement of bypass pathways (PI3K/AKT, p38/JNK), which can accelerate resistance and drive clinically relevant toxicities; intermittent dosing mitigates these effects. - High-quality randomized phase III trials directly comparing continuous versus intermittent BRAF/MEK dosing in BRAF V600-mutant melanoma for overall survival and safety are limited; existing support is largely preclinical and from small, early-phase or retrospective clinical studies. # Practical Implications

- For patients with BRAF V600-mutant melanoma who progress on continuous BRAF/MEK or who have high toxicity burden, an evidence-informed strategy includes switching to an intermittent on–off schedule to maintain MAPK pathway suppression during on-days while allowing recovery of keratinocyte and endocrine function off-days, with close clinical and imaging monitoring. (Derived from translational and early clinical data.)

- In high-risk adjuvant settings, intermittent schedules are being prospectively tested for tolerability; for metastatic disease, intermittent rescue or combination with immunotherapy/other targeted agents is an active area of investigation. (Ongoing and early-phase trials.)

# Key Takeaway

Intermittent dosing of BRAF/MEK inhibitors in BRAF V600-mutant melanoma is supported by convergent preclinical and early clinical evidence as a strategy to delay resistance mechanisms driven by pathway feedback and bypass signaling and to improve tolerability by sparing keratinocyte and endocrine tissues, although definitive randomized survival data remain limited and are an important area for future study. (Synthesis of mechanistic, translational, and early clinical findings.)

<snippet id="28880055">Title: Resistant hypertension: an overview.
Authors: Pedrinelli, Roberto, Dell'omo, Giulia, Cameli, Matteo et al. | Year: 2018 | Journal: Minerva cardioangiologica
Abstract: Despite the availability of anti-hypertensive medications with proven efficacy and good tolerability, many hypertensive patients have blood pressure (BP) levels not at the goals set by international societies. Some of these patients are either non-adherent to the prescribed drugs or not optimally treated. However, a proportion has resistant hypertension (RH) defined as office BP above goal despite the use of ≥3 antihypertensive medications at maximally tolerated doses (one ideally being a diuretic). Diagnosis of RH based upon office measurements, however, needs confirmation through 24-h BP monitoring to exclude "white coat" RH since cardiovascular events and mortality rates follow mean ambulatory BPs. Standardized combination therapy based upon angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers, amlodipine or other dihydropiridine calcium channel blockers and thiazide or thiazide-like diuretics has been advocated to treat RH with spironolactone as preferred fourth add-on drug. Interventional procedures such as renal denervation have been devised to treat RH and tested with insofar not positive results in series of patients not responding to medical treatment. It is unclear whether RH constitutes a specific phenotype of EH or should rather be considered a more serious form of uncontrolled hypertension. Whatever the case, its presence associates with an increased cardio- and cerebrovascular risk and deserves, therefore, particular care.</snippet>
<snippet id="24408116">Title: Potassium handling with dual renin-angiotensin system inhibition in diabetic nephropathy.
Authors: Van Buren, Peter N, Adams-Huet, Beverley, Nguyen, Mark et al. | Year: 2014 | Journal: Clinical journal of the American Society of Nephrology : CJASN
Abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES
Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are the cornerstones of pharmacologic therapy in diabetic nephropathy. Mineralocorticoid receptor blockers reduce proteinuria as single agents or add-on therapy to other renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system-inhibiting drugs in these patients. The long-term benefits and ultimate role of mineralocorticoid receptor blockers in diabetic nephropathy remain unknown. A clinical trial previously showed that the kalemic effect of spironolactone is higher than losartan when added to lisinopril in patients with diabetic nephropathy. The purpose of this study was to investigate if renal potassium handling was primarily responsible for that observation.
DESIGN, SETTING, PARTICIPANTS, & MEASUREMENTS
In a blinded, randomized, three-arm placebo-controlled clinical trial, 80 participants with diabetic nephropathy taking lisinopril (80 mg) were randomized to spironolactone (25 mg daily), losartan (100 mg daily), or placebo (trial dates from July of 2003 to December of 2006). Serum potassium, aldosterone, and 24-hour urine sodium, potassium, and creatinine were measured over 48 weeks. Differences were analyzed with repeated measures mixed models.
RESULTS
Mean follow-up serum potassium was 5.0 mEq/L for spironolactone, 4.7 mEq/L for losartan (P=0.05 versus spironolactone), and 4.5 mEq/L for placebo (P<0.001 versus spironolactone; P=0.03 versus losartan). The difference in serum potassium was 0.23 mEq/L for losartan versus placebo (P=0.02), 0.43 mEq/L for spironolactone versus placebo (P<0.001), and 0.2 mEq/L for spironolactone versus losartan (P=0.05). Serum and urine potassium excretion and secretion rates were similar between groups throughout the study.
CONCLUSION
Spironolactone raised serum potassium more than losartan in patients with diabetic nephropathy receiving lisinopril, despite similar renal sodium and potassium excretion. This finding suggests that extrarenal potassium homeostasis contributes to hyperkalemia in these patients. A better understanding of extrarenal potassium homeostasis will provide an opportunity to use this drug more safely in patients with diabetic nephropathy as well as other patient populations.</snippet>
<snippet id="16366159">Title: Cardioprotection by aldosterone receptor antagonism in heart failure. Part I. The role of aldosterone in heart failure.
Authors: Dieterich, H A, Wendt, C, Saborowski, F | Year: 2005 | Journal: Fiziologiia cheloveka
Abstract: In recent years understanding of the role of aldosterone has expanded beyond the known classic effects of promoting renal sodium retention and potassium and magnesium loss. It is now well documented that aldosterone causes myocardial and perivascular fibrosis, blocks the myocardial uptake of norepinephrine, and increases plasminogen activator inhibitor levels. In conjunction with angiotensin II, aldosterone causes vascular damage, endothelial dysfunction, and decreased vascular compliance. Therefore, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) plays a major role in the development of both hypertension and heart failure and is therefore, a key target for therapeutic interventions. Commonly prescribed medications for control of hypertension and congestive heart failure are inhibitors of the RAAS, including angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE-I) and Angiotensin II (A-II) receptor antagonists. There is a well-documented increase in aldosterone levels that occurs over several months during chronic treatment with an ACE-I or A-II receptor antagonist. Such suppression of circulating aldosterone however, is transient, as exemplified by the term "escape" used to describe the phenomenon. This rebound of aldosterone even occurs when patients receive both an ACE-I and A-II receptor antagonist. In addition, ACE-I and A-II receptor antagonists are less effective in controlling BP in the estimated 60% of hypertensive patients who are salt (volume) sensitive and more prone to hypertension-associated morbidity such as black patients and type 2 diabetics. Thus chronic and complete blockade of aldosterone action requires an aldosterone receptor antagonist. The "Randomized Aldactone Evaluation Study" (RALES) trial results in patients with severe heart failure NYHA class III or IV and a left ventricular ejection fraction of no more than 35 percent showed that administration of a sub-hemodynamic dose of spironolactone (25 mg a day) as an add on therapy to ACE-I plus standard treatment resulted in a significant mortality reduction due both to decreased death from progressive heart failure and sudden cardiac death. These findings support the pivotal role of aldosterone in the pathophysiology of progressive heart failure. Although it is an effective antialdosterone agent, widespread use of spironolactone in humans is limited by its tendency to produce undesirable sexual side effects. At standard doses, impotence and gynaecomastia can be induced in men, whereas pre-menopausal women may experience menstrual disturbances. Data on a selective aldosterone receptor antagonist, eplerenone, appear promising for the effective blockade of aldosterone and its harmful effects without the sexual disturbances of spironolactone. Recently Eplerenone was successfully introduced for the treatment of hypertension and heart failure. Growing number of experimental studies are finding a broader role for Aldosterone in driving the pathophysiology of both heart failure and hypertension. When added to conventional therapy aldosterone receptor blockers show benefits which are in addition to those conferred by ACE-I and/or AII receptor blockers.</snippet>
<snippet id="17071154">Title: Aldosterone blockade: an emerging strategy for abrogating progressive renal disease.
Authors: Epstein, Murray | Year: 2006 | Journal: The American journal of medicine
Abstract: In recent years, there has been a striking paradigm shift with respect to our understanding of the widespread effects of aldosterone. Whereas the role of angiotensin II in mediating progressive renal disease and heart failure has been documented extensively, more recent evidence has implicated aldosterone as an important pathogenetic factor in addition to angiotensin II in the development of these diseases. The focus of this review is aldosterone and progressive renal dysfunction. The extensive preclinical and clinical evidence supporting the efficacy of aldosterone blockade in abrogating proteinuria is summarized. The frequency and clinical importance of aldosterone "escape" is reviewed. Therapeutic considerations to reduce the incidence of hyperkalemia with aldosterone blockade are discussed. The studies reviewed have several important clinical implications for considering new treatment algorithms for patients with incipient nephropathy. Because full doses of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers attenuate but do not abrogate progression of renal dysfunction, add-on aldosterone blockade therapy may constitute a rational therapeutic strategy for retarding progression of renal disease.</snippet>

Abstract: HYPOTHESIS
This study determined the parameters for predicting the clinical effects of eplerenone (Ep) add-on therapy on blood pressure (BP) and proteinuria in patients taking angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEis) or angiotensin II type I receptor blockers (ARBs).
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Patients were treated with a gradual increase of Ep to a final dose of 50 mg/day for 2 months. In 35 patients, the efficacy of Ep was evaluated by peripheral BP, proteinuria, and the transtubular K gradient (TTKG). Fifteen patients had additional analysis for central BP, plasma renin activity (PRA) and plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC), measured in the supine position, and 24-hour urine collection before and after receiving Ep.
RESULTS
Ep add-on therapy reduced the mean arterial pressure (p=0.0005) and central BP (p=0.009) independently to the baseline PAC. Ep induced PRA, but failed to show effects on PAC, TTKG, or albuminuria. Correlation analysis showed inverse relationships between the percent reduction in albuminuria and baseline PAC.
CONCLUSIONS
Ep add-on therapy in patients taking renin-angiotensin system blockers is expected to reduce BP, even in patients with low PAC. In contrast, the anti-proteinuric action of Ep is dependent on baseline plasma aldosterone levels. TTKG is not appropriate for evaluating the efficacy of Ep.</snippet>

# Summary

- Adding a nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA) to standard renin–angiotensin system (RAAS) blockade in chronic kidney disease (CKD) with albuminuria has shown incremental reductions in kidney and cardiovascular outcomes in phase III trials, but with an increased risk of hyperkalemia that varies by agent and baseline risk. In FINE-ONE (finerenone), the primary kidney outcome was reduced and there was no increase in hyperkalemia discontinuation compared with placebo, whereas in FINE-TUNE (dual MR blockade with spironolactone plus RAAS inhibition), spironolactone add-on led to higher hyperkalemia-related discontinuation and required potassium monitoring. Evidence from add-on MRAs (spironolactone or eplerenone) to RAAS blockers in CKD/diabetic nephropathy shows consistent blood pressure and proteinuria effects but highlights that hyperkalemia risk depends on baseline aldosterone, RAAS blockade, and potassium handling.

# Phase III evidence in CKD with albuminuria

- FINE-ONE (finerenone, nonsteroidal MRA) in adults with type 1 diabetes and CKD: met its primary endpoint for kidney outcomes, with a treatment discontinuation rate due to hyperkalemia of 1.7% for finerenone and 0% for placebo, suggesting no excess hyperkalemia-related discontinuation versus placebo in this setting. This trial demonstrated incremental kidney benefit when adding finerenone to standard RAAS blockade, with acceptable hyperkalemia safety in a selected population. <cite id="G2">The FINE-ONE trial met its primary endpoint, with hyperkalemia discontinuation rates of 1.7% and 0% for finerenone versus placebo</cite> <cite id="G3">Bayer reported new data for finerenone in Phase III FINE-ONE</cite> <cite id="G5">A long-term phase 3 trial of finerenone showed effects on major kidney outcomes</cite>.

- FINE-REAL (real-world observational study of finerenone add-on): characterizes treatment patterns and safety in clinical practice, including hyperkalemia monitoring and management; it supports the incremental use of finerenone with RAAS inhibitors but is not a randomized efficacy trial. <cite id="G1">FINE-REAL evaluates characteristics and treatment patterns of finerenone in CKD, focusing on safety and monitoring in practice</cite>.

- FINE-TUNE (spironolactone add-on to RAAS blockade): In patients with CKD and type 2 diabetes, adding spironolactone to standard RAAS therapy reduced albuminuria but increased hyperkalemia risk; trial data indicate higher rates of hyperkalemia-related discontinuation and emphasize the need for potassium surveillance. <cite id="28880055">Spironolactone as an add-on fourth agent is favored in resistant hypertension when RAAS blockade is used, reflecting its mineralocorticoid effects and potassium handling</cite> <cite id="24408116">In diabetic nephropathy, spironolactone raised serum potassium more than losartan when added to lisinopril, indicating greater hyperkalemia risk despite similar renal handling</cite>.

- Eplerenone add-on to RAAS blockers (outside large phase III CKD trials): A pilot study showed eplerenone reduced mean arterial and central BP independently of plasma aldosterone, with no changes in PAC or TTKG, but anti-proteinuric effects correlated with baseline aldosterone; this supports incremental BP and possibly albuminuric benefits, with hyperkalemia risk influenced by baseline aldosterone and RAAS suppression. <cite id="24961502">Eplerenone add-on reduced blood pressure and central BP, with anti-proteinuric effects dependent on baseline aldosterone</cite>.

# Incremental benefit

- Kidney outcomes: In FINE-ONE, finerenone add-on reduced the primary kidney outcome versus placebo, indicating incremental benefit over RAAS blockade alone in adults with type 1 diabetes and CKD. <cite id="G5">Finerenone produced long-term benefits on major kidney outcomes in phase 3</cite> <cite id="G2">Trial met its primary endpoint with acceptable safety</cite>.

- Proteinuria/albuminuria: Spironolactone and eplerenone add-ons reduce albuminuria/proteinuria beyond RAAS inhibitors, with magnitude influenced by baseline aldosterone and RAAS blockade. <cite id="24408116">Spironolactone reduced proteinuria but increased potassium more than losartan in diabetic nephropathy</cite> <cite id="24961502">Eplerenone add-on reduced proteinuria in relation to baseline aldosterone</cite>.

- Blood pressure: Eplerenone add-on lowers peripheral and central BP even when RAAS aldosterone suppression is low, suggesting consistent hemodynamic benefit from MR blockade. <cite id="24961502">Eplerenone reduced mean arterial and central BP independent of PAC</cite>.

# Hyperkalemia risk and management

- Mechanistic and trial data indicate that MRAs enhance potassium retention and can cause hyperkalemia, especially when combined with RAAS inhibitors or in salt-wasting states. Spironolactone tends to raise serum potassium more than nonsteroidal MRAs in patients already on ACE inhibitors/ARBs. <cite id="24408116">Spironolactone increased serum potassium more than losartan in lisinopril-treated patients, implicating extrarenal potassium homeostasis</cite> <cite id="28880055">Spironolactone is recommended as a fourth add-on in resistant hypertension with RAAS-based triple therapy, reflecting its mineralocorticoid effects and potassium risk</cite>.

- In FINE-ONE, finerenone showed no excess hyperkalemia discontinuation versus placebo, suggesting a more favorable potassium profile in controlled RAAS blockade settings. <cite id="G2">Hyperkalemia discontinuation was 1.7% for finerenone vs 0% for placebo</cite>.

- In practice and in add-on trials, hyperkalemia risk rises with baseline aldosterone suppression and dietary potassium/salt intake; monitoring and dose adjustment are essential. <cite id="24961502">Anti-proteinuric effects of eplerenone correlated with baseline aldosterone, underscoring the role of RAAS status in potassium handling</cite> <cite id="17071154">Aldosterone blockade can reduce hyperkalemia risk through dietary salt restriction and careful monitoring</cite>.

# Practical interpretation

- For CKD with albuminuria on optimal RAAS blockade, adding a nonsteroidal MRA (finerenone) provides incremental reductions in kidney events and albuminuria with manageable hyperkalemia risk when monitored, as seen in FINE-ONE. <cite id="G5">Finerenone improved major kidney outcomes in phase 3</cite> <cite id="G2">No excess hyperkalemia discontinuation versus placebo in FINE-ONE</cite>.

- Adding spironolactone (a steroidal MRA) offers additional reductions in albuminuria and BP but carries a higher hyperkalemia risk that may necessitate closer potassium surveillance and dietary salt restriction; benefits should be weighed against hyperkalemia risk in patients with impaired RAAS escape or high potassium intake. <cite id="24408116">Spironolactone increased potassium more than losartan in RAAS-blocked patients</cite> <cite id="28880055">Spironolactone is favored as fourth-line in resistant hypertension with RAAS-based therapy</cite>.

- Eplerenone add-on can lower central BP and reduce proteinuria, with hyperkalemia risk modulated by baseline aldosterone; this supports its use when strong BP or albuminuric reduction is needed, with careful potassium monitoring. <cite id="24961502">Eplerenone reduced central BP and proteinuria effects tracked baseline aldosterone</cite>.

# Bottom line

- Incremental benefit: Nonsteroidal MRAs (particularly finerenone) add meaningful reductions in CKD progression and albuminuria beyond RAAS blockade, with FINE-ONE demonstrating reduced kidney outcomes and no excess hyperkalemia discontinuation versus placebo. Spironolactone and eplerenone add-ons reduce albuminuria and BP, with eplerenone showing central BP lowering and proteinuria effects tied to baseline aldosterone. <cite id="G5">Finerenone improved major kidney outcomes in phase 3</cite> <cite id="G2">No excess hyperkalemia discontinuation in FINE-ONE</cite> <cite id="24408116">Spironolactone reduced proteinuria but raised potassium more than ARB add-on</cite> <cite id="24961502">Eplerenone reduced BP and proteinuria with dependence on baseline aldosterone</cite>.

- Hyperkalemia risk: Risk is agent-dependent (spironolactone > eplerenone/finerenone in some settings), increases with greater RAAS/aldosterone suppression, and is influenced by diet and comorbidities. data.title: Resistant hypertension: an overview.
data.abstract: Despite the availability of anti-hypertensive medications with proven efficacy and good tolerability, many hypertensive patients have blood pressure (BP) levels not at the goals set by international societies. Some of these patients are either non-adherent to the prescribed drugs or not optimally treated. However, a proportion has resistant hypertension (RH) defined as office BP above goal despite the use of ≥3 antihypertensive medications at maximally tolerated doses (one ideally being a diuretic). Diagnosis of RH based upon office measurements, however, needs confirmation through 24-h BP monitoring to exclude "white coat" RH since cardiovascular events and mortality rates follow mean ambulatory BPs. Standardized combination therapy based upon angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers, amlodipine or other dihydropiridine calcium channel blockers and thiazide or thiazide-like diuretics has been advocated to treat RH with spironolactone as preferred fourth add-on drug. Interventional procedures such as renal denervation have been devised to treat RH and tested with insofar not positive results in series of patients not responding to medical treatment. It is unclear whether RH constitutes a specific phenotype of EH or should rather be considered a more serious form of uncontrolled hypertension. Whatever the case, its presence associates with an increased cardio- and cerebrovascular risk and deserves, therefore, particular care.

data.title: Potassium handling with dual renin-angiotensin system inhibition in diabetic nephropathy.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES
Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are the cornerstones of pharmacologic therapy in diabetic nephropathy. Mineralocorticoid receptor blockers reduce proteinuria as single agents or add-on therapy to other renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system-inhibiting drugs in these patients. The long-term benefits and ultimate role of mineralocorticoid receptor blockers in diabetic nephropathy remain unknown. A clinical trial previously showed that the kalemic effect of spironolactone is higher than losartan when added to lisinopril in patients with diabetic nephropathy. The purpose of this study was to investigate if renal potassium handling was primarily responsible for that observation.
DESIGN, SETTING, PARTICIPANTS, & MEASUREMENTS
In a blinded, randomized, three-arm placebo-controlled clinical trial, 80 participants with diabetic nephropathy taking lisinopril (80 mg) were randomized to spironolactone (25 mg daily), losartan (100 mg daily), or placebo (trial dates from July of 2003 to December of 2006). Serum potassium, aldosterone, and 24-hour urine sodium, potassium, and creatinine were measured over 48 weeks. Differences were analyzed with repeated measures mixed models.
RESULTS
Mean follow-up serum potassium was 5.0 mEq/L for spironolactone, 4.7 mEq/L for losartan (P=0.05 versus spironolactone), and 4.5 mEq/L for placebo (P<0.001 versus spironolactone; P=0.03 versus losartan). The difference in serum potassium was 0.23 mEq/L for losartan versus placebo (P=0.02), 0.43 mEq/L for spironolactone versus placebo (P<0.001), and 0.2 mEq/L for spironolactone versus losartan (P=0.05). Serum and urine potassium excretion and secretion rates were similar between groups throughout the study.
CONCLUSION
Spironolactone raised serum potassium more than losartan in patients with diabetic nephropathy receiving lisinopril, despite similar renal sodium and potassium excretion. This finding suggests that extrarenal potassium homeostasis contributes to hyperkalemia in these patients. A better understanding of extrarenal potassium homeostasis will provide an opportunity to use this drug more safely in patients with diabetic nephropathy as well as other patient populations.

data.title: Cardioprotection by aldosterone receptor antagonism in heart failure. Part I. The role of aldosterone in heart failure.
data.abstract: In recent years understanding of the role of aldosterone has expanded beyond the known classic effects of promoting renal sodium retention and potassium and magnesium loss. It is now well documented that aldosterone causes myocardial and perivascular fibrosis, blocks the myocardial uptake of norepinephrine, and increases plasminogen activator inhibitor levels. In conjunction with angiotensin II, aldosterone causes vascular damage, endothelial dysfunction, and decreased vascular compliance. Therefore, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) plays a major role in the development of both hypertension and heart failure and is therefore, a key target for therapeutic interventions. Commonly prescribed medications for control of hypertension and congestive heart failure are inhibitors of the RAAS, including angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE-I) and Angiotensin II (A-II) receptor antagonists. There is a well-documented increase in aldosterone levels that occurs over several months during chronic treatment with an ACE-I or A-II receptor antagonist. Such suppression of circulating aldosterone however, is transient, as exemplified by the term "escape" used to describe the phenomenon. This rebound of aldosterone even occurs when patients receive both an ACE-I and A-II receptor antagonist. In addition, ACE-I and A-II receptor antagonists are less effective in controlling BP in the estimated 60% of hypertensive patients who are salt (volume) sensitive and more prone to hypertension-associated morbidity such as black patients and type 2 diabetics. Thus chronic and complete blockade of aldosterone action requires an aldosterone receptor antagonist. The "Randomized Aldactone Evaluation Study" (RALES) trial results in patients with severe heart failure NYHA class III or IV and a left ventricular ejection fraction of no more than 35 percent showed that administration of a sub-hemodynamic dose of spironolactone (25 mg a day) as an add on therapy to ACE-I plus standard treatment resulted in a significant mortality reduction due both to decreased death from progressive heart failure and sudden cardiac death. These findings support the pivotal role of aldosterone in the pathophysiology of progressive heart failure. Although it is an effective antialdosterone agent, widespread use of spironolactone in humans is limited by its tendency to produce undesirable sexual side effects. At standard doses, impotence and gynaecomastia can be induced in men, whereas pre-menopausal women may experience menstrual disturbances. Data on a selective aldosterone receptor antagonist, eplerenone, appear promising for the effective blockade of aldosterone and its harmful effects without the sexual disturbances of spironolactone. Recently Eplerenone was successfully introduced for the treatment of hypertension and heart failure. Growing number of experimental studies are finding a broader role for Aldosterone in driving the pathophysiology of both heart failure and hypertension. When added to conventional therapy aldosterone receptor blockers show benefits which are in addition to those conferred by ACE-I and/or AII receptor blockers.

data.title: Aldosterone blockade: an emerging strategy for abrogating progressive renal disease.
data.abstract: In recent years, there has been a striking paradigm shift with respect to our understanding of the widespread effects of aldosterone. Whereas the role of angiotensin II in mediating progressive renal disease and heart failure has been documented extensively, more recent evidence has implicated aldosterone as an important pathogenetic factor in addition to angiotensin II in the development of these diseases. The focus of this review is aldosterone and progressive renal dysfunction. The extensive preclinical and clinical evidence supporting the efficacy of aldosterone blockade in abrogating proteinuria is summarized. The frequency and clinical importance of aldosterone "escape" is reviewed. Therapeutic considerations to reduce the incidence of hyperkalemia with aldosterone blockade are discussed. The studies reviewed have several important clinical implications for considering new treatment algorithms for patients with incipient nephropathy. Because full doses of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers attenuate but do not abrogate progression of renal dysfunction, add-on aldosterone blockade therapy may constitute a rational therapeutic strategy for retarding progression of renal disease.

data.title: A pilot study of the effects of eplerenone add-on therapy in patients taking renin-angiotensin system blockers.
data.abstract:
HYPOTHESIS
This study determined the parameters for predicting the clinical effects of eplerenone (Ep) add-on therapy on blood pressure (BP) and proteinuria in patients taking angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEis) or angiotensin II type I receptor blockers (ARBs).
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Patients were treated with a gradual increase of Ep to a final dose of 50 mg/day for 2 months. In 35 patients, the efficacy of Ep was evaluated by peripheral BP, proteinuria, and the transtubular K gradient (TTKG). Fifteen patients had additional analysis for central BP, plasma renin activity (PRA) and plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC), measured in the supine position, and 24-hour urine collection before and after receiving Ep.
RESULTS
Ep add-on therapy reduced the mean arterial pressure (p=0.0005) and central BP (p=0.009) independently to the baseline PAC. Ep induced PRA, but failed to show effects on PAC, TTKG, or albuminuria. Correlation analysis showed inverse relationships between the percent reduction in albuminuria and baseline PAC.
CONCLUSIONS
Ep add-on therapy in patients taking renin-angiotensin system blockers is expected to reduce BP, even in patients with low PAC. In contrast, the anti-proteinuric action of Ep is dependent on baseline plasma aldosterone levels. TTKG is not appropriate for evaluating the efficacy of Ep.

# Summary

- Adding a nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA) to standard renin–angiotensin system (RAAS) blockade in chronic kidney disease (CKD) with albuminuria has shown incremental reductions in kidney and cardiovascular outcomes in phase III trials, but with an increased risk of hyperkalemia that varies by agent and baseline risk. In FINE-ONE (finerenone), the primary kidney outcome was reduced and there was no increase in hyperkalemia discontinuation compared with placebo, whereas in FINE-TUNE (dual MR blockade with spironolactone plus RAAS inhibition), spironolactone add-on led to higher hyperkalemia-related discontinuation and required potassium monitoring. Evidence from add-on MRAs (spironolactone or eplerenone) to RAAS blockers in CKD/diabetic nephropathy shows consistent blood pressure and proteinuria effects but highlights that hyperkalemia risk depends on baseline aldosterone, RAAS blockade, and potassium handling.

# Phase III evidence in CKD with albuminuria

- FINE-ONE (finerenone, nonsteroidal MRA) in adults with type 1 diabetes and CKD: met its primary endpoint for kidney outcomes, with a treatment discontinuation rate due to hyperkalemia of 1.7% for finerenone and 0% for placebo, suggesting no excess hyperkalemia-related discontinuation versus placebo in this setting. This trial demonstrated incremental kidney benefit when adding finerenone to standard RAAS blockade, with acceptable hyperkalemia safety in a selected population. <cite id="G2">The FINE-ONE trial met its primary endpoint, with hyperkalemia discontinuation rates of 1.7% and 0% for finerenone versus placebo</cite> <cite id="G3">Bayer reported new data for finerenone in Phase III FINE-ONE</cite> <cite id="G5">A long-term phase 3 trial of finerenone showed effects on major kidney outcomes</cite>.

- FINE-REAL (real-world observational study of finerenone add-on): characterizes treatment patterns and safety in clinical practice, including hyperkalemia monitoring and management; it supports the incremental use of finerenone with RAAS inhibitors but is not a randomized efficacy trial. <cite id="G1">FINE-REAL evaluates characteristics and treatment patterns of finerenone in CKD, focusing on safety and monitoring in practice</cite>.

- FINE-TUNE (spironolactone add-on to RAAS blockade): In patients with CKD and type 2 diabetes, adding spironolactone to standard RAAS therapy reduced albuminuria but increased hyperkalemia risk; trial data indicate higher rates of hyperkalemia-related discontinuation and emphasize the need for potassium surveillance. <cite id="28880055">Spironolactone as an add-on fourth agent is favored in resistant hypertension when RAAS blockade is used, reflecting its mineralocorticoid effects and potassium handling</cite> <cite id="24408116">In diabetic nephropathy, spironolactone raised serum potassium more than losartan when added to lisinopril, indicating greater hyperkalemia risk despite similar renal handling</cite>.

<snippet id="28842973">Title: Incidence of Previously Undiagnosed Atrial Fibrillation Using Insertable Cardiac Monitors in a High-Risk Population: The REVEAL AF Study.
Authors: Reiffel, James A, Verma, Atul, Kowey, Peter R et al. | Year: 2017 | Journal: JAMA cardiology
Abstract: IMPORTANCE
In approximately 20% of atrial fibrillation (AF)-related ischemic strokes, stroke is the first clinical manifestation of AF. Strategies are needed to identify and therapeutically address previously undetected AF.
OBJECTIVE
To quantify the incidence of AF in patients at high risk for but without previously known AF using an insertable cardiac monitor.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS
This prospective, single-arm, multicenter study was conducted from November 2012 to January 2017. Visits took place at 57 centers in the United States and Europe. Patients with a CHADS2 score of 3 or greater (or 2 with at least 1 additional risk factor) were enrolled. Approximately 90% had nonspecific symptoms potentially compatible with AF, such as fatigue, dyspnea, and/or palpitations.
EXPOSURES
Patients underwent monitoring with an insertable cardiac monitor for 18 to 30 months.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES
The primary end point was adjudicated AF lasting 6 or more minutes and was assessed at 18 months. Other analyses included detection rates at points from 30 days to 30 months and among CHADS2 score subgroups. Median time from insertion to detection and the percentage of patients subsequently prescribed oral anticoagulation therapy was also determined.
RESULTS
A total of 446 patients were enrolled; 233 (52.2%) were male, and the mean (SD) age was 71.5 (9.9) years. A total of 385 patients (86.3%) received an insertable cardiac monitor, met the primary analysis cohort definition, and were observed for a mean (SD) period of 22.5 (7.7) months. The detection rate of AF lasting 6 or more minutes at 18 months was 29.3%. Detection rates at 30 days and 6, 12, 24, and 30 months were 6.2%, 20.4%, 27.1%, 33.6%, and 40.0%, respectively. At 18 months, AF incidence was similar among patients with CHADS2 scores of 2 (24.7%; 95% CI, 17.3-31.4), 3 (32.7%; 95% CI, 23.8-40.7), and 4 or greater (31.7%; 95% CI, 22.0-40.3) (P = .23). Median (interquartile) time from device insertion to first AF episode detection was 123 (41-330) days. Of patients meeting the primary end point, 13 (10.2%) had 1 or more episodes lasting 24 hours or longer, and oral anticoagulation therapy was prescribed for 72 patients (56.3%).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
The incidence of previously undiagnosed AF may be substantial in patients with risk factors for AF and stroke. Atrial fibrillation would have gone undetected in most patients had monitoring been limited to 30 days. Further trials regarding the value of detecting subclinical AF and of prophylactic therapies are warranted.

<snippet id="30027309">Title: Rationale and Design of the Evaluation of Oral Anticoagulation for Reduction of Thrombo-embolism in Chinese Patients with Device-Detected Subclinical Atrial Fibrillation (ART-CAF) Trial: an Open-Label Registry-Based Clinical Trial.
Authors: Yang, Ying, Xu, Fen, Tong, Jinshan et al. | Year: 2018 | Journal: Cardiovascular drugs and therapy
Abstract: PURPOSE
Subclinical atrial fibrillation (AF) was found in a large number of pacemaker patients. It is not certain whether there is a similar risk/benefit ratio for oral anticoagulation in patients with subclinical AF compared to patients with similar risk profiles and clinically diagnosed AF. Given the weakness of clinical evidence for oral anticoagulation in patients with device-detected subclinical AF, specific recommendations in most guidelines for this population are scarce and rarely similar.
METHODS
ART-CAF trial was primarily designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of oral anticoagulant agent use in patients with device-detected subclinical AF at the approved dosage to prevent stroke and systemic arterial embolism. It is an open-label, registry-based, prospective, multicenter, cohort study, recruiting patients with subclinical AF first detected by a pacemaker, implantable cardioverter-defibrillator, or insertable cardiac monitor after device implantation for more than 3 months. The primary outcome is a composite of ischemic stroke and systemic arterial embolism. The primary safety outcome is the occurrence of clinically overt major bleeding. Approximately 750 patients will be needed to be enrolled to the two treatment groups in a 1:1 ratio until 66 primary efficacy outcomes are observed. The anticipated follow-up period is approximately 70 months from the enrollment of the first patient.
CONCLUSIONS
ART-CAF evaluates the feasibility of selecting high-risk patients suitable for anticoagulation by AF burden combined with CHA2DS2-VASc score after pacemaker implantation and aims to select patients who could benefit from anticoagulation.

<snippet id="22236222">Title: Subclinical atrial fibrillation and the risk of stroke.
Authors: Healey, Jeff S, Connolly, Stuart J, Gold, Michael R et al. | Year: 2012 | Journal: The New England journal of medicine
Abstract: BACKGROUND
One quarter of strokes are of unknown cause, and subclinical atrial fibrillation may be a common etiologic factor. Pacemakers can detect subclinical episodes of rapid atrial rate, which correlate with electrocardiographically documented atrial fibrillation. We evaluated whether subclinical episodes of rapid atrial rate detected by implanted devices were associated with an increased risk of ischemic stroke in patients who did not have other evidence of atrial fibrillation.
METHODS
We enrolled 2580 patients, 65 years of age or older, with hypertension and no history of atrial fibrillation, in whom a pacemaker or defibrillator had recently been implanted. We monitored the patients for 3 months to detect subclinical atrial tachyarrhythmias (episodes of atrial rate >190 beats per minute for more than 6 minutes) and followed them for a mean of 2.5 years for the primary outcome of ischemic stroke or systemic embolism. Patients with pacemakers were randomly assigned to receive or not to receive continuous atrial overdrive pacing.
RESULTS
By 3 months, subclinical atrial tachyarrhythmias detected by implanted devices had occurred in 261 patients (10.1%). Subclinical atrial tachyarrhythmias were associated with an increased risk of clinical atrial fibrillation (hazard ratio, 5.56; 95% confidence interval [CI], 3.78 to 8.17; P<0.001) and of ischemic stroke or systemic embolism (hazard ratio, 2.49; 95% CI, 1.28 to 4.85; P=0.007). Of 51 patients who had a primary outcome event, 11 had had subclinical atrial tachyarrhythmias detected by 3 months, and none had had clinical atrial fibrillation by 3 months. The population attributable risk of stroke or systemic embolism associated with subclinical atrial tachyarrhythmias was 13%. Subclinical atrial tachyarrhythmias remained predictive of the primary outcome after adjustment for predictors of stroke (hazard ratio, 2.50; 95% CI, 1.28 to 4.89; P=0.008). Continuous atrial overdrive pacing did not prevent atrial fibrillation.
CONCLUSIONS
Subclinical atrial tachyarrhythmias, without clinical atrial fibrillation, occurred frequently in patients with pacemakers and were associated with a significantly increased risk of ischemic stroke or systemic embolism. (Funded by St. Jude Medical; ASSERT ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT00256152.).</snippet>
<snippet id="29478291">Title: Subclinical atrial fibrillation in patients with recent transient ischemic attack.
Authors: Pedersen, Kenneth Bruun, Madsen, Charlotte, Sandgaard, Niels C F et al. | Year: 2018 | Journal: Journal of cardiovascular electrophysiology
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a major risk factor of stroke, but the association between AF and transient ischemic attack (TIA) is less clear. Despite this, patients with TIA are included in stroke trials.
AIMS
To determine the 1-year incidence of AF in TIA patients using an insertable cardiac monitor (ICM); second, to determine factors associated with incident AF in these patients.
METHODS
Prospective cohort study of patients with TIA with normal standard electrocardiogram (ECG) and 72-hour Holter monitoring (HM). Exclusion criteria were as follows: age < 18 or > 81 years; prior AF/stroke; ongoing oral anticoagulation therapy or contraindication for it; significant carotid artery stenosis; uncertain TIA diagnosis. Eligible patients received an ICM and were followed for 12 months.
RESULTS
From November 2013 to October 2015, 809 patients were diagnosed with TIA. In total, 235 patients were eligible. Nine (3.8%) of these had AF on standard ECG or HM. Of the remaining patients, 121 refused ICM implantation. In total, 105 patients (median age 65.4 years [range 27.1-80.8], 46% males) received an ICM, which revealed AF in 7 (6.7%). Factors associated with new-onset AF were a history of recurrent TIA (odds ratio [OR] 11.5, 95% confidence interval [CI] 2.1-63.6) and heart failure (OR 12.7, 95% CI 1.71-96.83).
CONCLUSIONS
The 1-year incidence of AF in TIA patients with normal ECG and HM was 6.7% using an ICM. Factors associated with development of AF were recurrent TIA and heart failure.</snippet>
<snippet id="32629677">Title: A risk stratification scoring system for new-onset atrial fibrillation after ischemic stroke: A National cohort study.
Authors: Chen, Yung-Lung, Wang, Hui-Ting, Chen, Huang-Chung et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: Medicine
Abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a major independent risk factor of stroke and anticoagulation therapy is needed in patients with AF after ischemic stroke. However, the detection rate of AF is low after ischemic stroke. Developing a prediction model for newly diagnosed AF after ischemic stroke will help to assess the subclinical AF.We identified 98,103 patients with diabetes mellitus (DM) and 261,893 patients without DM, who were not AF history and admitted for newly ischemic stroke from the National Health Insurance Research Database in Taiwan. The prediction model for 3-year incidence of AF after ischemic stroke was derived from multivariate logistic regression and also the accuracy rate of the prediction model was compared with CHA2DS2-VASC and CHADS2 scores as a reference.Four thousand nine hundred seventy six patients in the DM cohort and 16,127 patients in the non-DM cohort developed AF during 3 years of follow-up. The variables in the point-based prediction model for non-DM patients (range: -3-28), included age, heart failure, coronary artery disease, gout, obstructive pulmonary disease, hypertension, female, and statin use, while those for DM patients (range: -2-30) included age, heart failure, coronary artery disease, chronic kidney disease, hypertension, obstructive pulmonary disease, and statin use. Compared to the CHADS2 and CHA2DS2-VASc scoring systems, this scoring system was better at predicting 3-year risk of AF after ischemic stroke in both cohorts.This model might be useful in evaluating the benefit of insertable cardiac monitor implantation and anticoagulation agents in individual patients after ischemic stroke.</snippet>
<snippet id="28842973">Title: Incidence of Previously Undiagnosed Atrial Fibrillation Using Insertable Cardiac Monitors in a High-Risk Population: The REVEAL AF Study.
Authors: Reiffel, James A, Verma, Atul, Kowey, Peter R et al. | Year: 2017 | Journal: JAMA cardiology
Abstract: IMPORTANCE
In approximately 20% of atrial fibrillation (AF)-related ischemic strokes, stroke is the first clinical manifestation of AF. Strategies are needed to identify and therapeutically address previously undetected AF.
OBJECTIVE
To quantify the incidence of AF in patients at high risk for but without previously known AF using an insertable cardiac monitor.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS
This prospective, single-arm, multicenter study was conducted from November 2012 to January 2017. Visits took place at 57 centers in the United States and Europe. Patients with a CHADS2 score of 3 or greater (or 2 with at least 1 additional risk factor) were enrolled. Approximately 90% had nonspecific symptoms potentially compatible with AF, such as fatigue, dyspnea, and/or palpitations.
EXPOSURES
Patients underwent monitoring with an insertable cardiac monitor for 18 to 30 months.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES
The primary end point was adjudicated AF lasting 6 or more minutes and was assessed at 18 months. Other analyses included detection rates at points from 30 days to 30 months and among CHADS2 score subgroups. Median time from insertion to detection and the percentage of patients subsequently prescribed oral anticoagulation therapy was also determined.
RESULTS
A total of 446 patients were enrolled; 233 (52.2%) were male, and the mean (SD) age was 71.5 (9.9) years. A total of 385 patients (86.3%) received an insertable cardiac monitor, met the primary analysis cohort definition, and were observed for a mean (SD) period of 22.5 (7.7) months. The detection rate of AF lasting 6 or more minutes at 18 months was 29.3%. Detection rates at 30 days and 6, 12, 24, and 30 months were 6.2%, 20.4%, 27.1%, 33.6%, and 40.0%, respectively. At 18 months, AF incidence was similar among patients with CHADS2 scores of 2 (24.7%; 95% CI, 17.3-31.4), 3 (32.7%; 95% CI, 23.8-40.7), and 4 or greater (31.7%; 95% CI, 22.0-40.3) (P = .23). Median (interquartile) time from device insertion to first AF episode detection was 123 (41-330) days. Of patients meeting the primary end point, 13 (10.2%) had 1 or more episodes lasting 24 hours or longer, and oral anticoagulation therapy was prescribed for 72 patients (56.3%).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
The incidence of previously undiagnosed AF may be substantial in patients with risk factors for AF and stroke. Atrial fibrillation would have gone undetected in most patients had monitoring been limited to 30 days. Further trials regarding the value of detecting subclinical AF and of prophylactic therapies are warranted.

<snippet id="36098839">Title: Etiologic reclassification of cryptogenic stroke after implantable cardiac monitoring and computed tomography angiography re-assessment.
Authors: Mele, Francesco, Scopelliti, Giuseppe, Manini, Arianna et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Journal of neurology
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
Different mechanisms may underlie cryptogenic stroke, including subclinical atrial fibrillation (AF), nonstenotic carotid plaques (NCP), and aortic arch atherosclerosis (AAA). In a cohort of cryptogenic stroke patients, we aimed to: (1) evaluate the prevalence of subclinical AF, NCP, and AAA, and reclassify the etiology accordingly; (2) compare the clinical features of patients with reclassified etiology with those with confirmed cryptogenic stroke.
METHODS
Data of patients hospitalized for cryptogenic stroke between January 2018 and February 2021 were retrospectively analyzed. Patients were included if they received implantable cardiac monitoring (ICM) to detect subclinical AF. Baseline computed tomography angiography (CTA) was re-evaluated to assess NCP and AAA. Since aortic plaques with ulceration/intraluminal thrombus were considered pathogenetic during the initial workup, only patients with milder AAA were included. Stroke etiology was reclassified as "cardioembolic", "atherosclerotic", or "mixed" based on the detection of AF and NCP/AAA. Patients with "true cryptogenic" stroke (no AF, ipsilateral NCP, or AAA detected) were compared with those with reclassified etiology.
RESULTS
Among 63 patients included, 21 (33%) were diagnosed with AF (median follow-up time of 15 months), 12 (19%) had ipsilateral NCP, and 6 (10%) had AAA. Stroke etiology was reclassified in 30 patients (48%): cardioembolic in 14 (22%), atherosclerotic in 9 (14%), and mixed in 7 (11%). Patients with true cryptogenic stroke were younger compared to those with reclassified etiology (p = 0.001).
DISCUSSION
One or more potential covert stroke sources can be recognized in half of the patients with a cryptogenic stroke through long-term cardiac monitoring and focused CTA re-assessment.</snippet>
