# Summary

- Subclinical atrial fibrillation (AF) and other subclinical atrial tachyarrhythmias detected by implanted cardiac devices are associated with a higher risk of ischemic stroke or systemic embolism in patients without a prior diagnosis of AF. In the ASSERT trial, episodes of rapid atrial rate (>190 bpm for ≥6 minutes) detected by pacemakers/ICDs predicted subsequent ischemic stroke or systemic embolism (hazard ratio 2.49, 95% CI 1.28–4.85) and were linked to a 13% population attributable risk for stroke/systemic embolism; AF burden remained predictive after adjustment for stroke risk factors (HR 2.50, 95% CI 1.28–4.89) and continuous atrial overdrive pacing did not prevent AF or stroke in this setting. <cite id="22236222">Subclinical atrial tachyarrhythmias were associated with an increased risk of ischemic stroke or systemic embolism (HR 2.49; 95% CI, 1.28 to 4.85) and a population attributable risk of 13%, and remained predictive after adjustment for stroke predictors (HR 2.50; 95% CI, 1.28 to 4.89); continuous atrial overdrive pacing did not prevent atrial fibrillation</cite>.

- Observational cohorts and registry designs corroborate that device-detected subclinical AF is common in high-risk patients and that AF detected by devices predicts adverse cerebrovascular outcomes. Insertable cardiac monitors identify substantial previously undiagnosed AF in patients with high CHADS2 scores, and many such patients subsequently receive anticoagulation; AF detection on devices is also more frequent in patients with cryptogenic stroke than initially apparent, supporting a causal link between subclinical arrhythmia and thromboembolic events. <cite id="28842973">In high-risk patients (CHADS2 ≥3), insertable cardiac monitors detected AF in 86.3% meeting the primary cohort definition over a mean 22.5 months, with rising detection rates over time (40% by 30 months), and many patients subsequently started on oral anticoagulation</cite>. <cite id="36098839">In a cohort of cryptogenic stroke patients, long-term cardiac monitoring detected AF in 33% and combined findings reclassified etiology away from cryptogenic in 48%, supporting a role for subclinical AF in stroke pathogenesis</cite>.

- Evidence in specific populations (e.g., TIA and amyloidosis) shows that device-detected or device-incident AF is common and that anticoagulation after device detection is associated with no ischemic strokes in follow-up, reinforcing the clinical importance of AF burden detected by devices. <cite id="29478291">In TIA patients with normal standard ECG and Holter, insertable cardiac monitors detected incident AF in 6.7% over 1 year, with risk factors including recurrent TIA and heart failure</cite>. <cite id="35439584">In transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis, routine monitoring or device interrogation uncovered AF/AFL in half of patients without prior diagnosis, and ischemic strokes occurred in 11% overall but none among those on anticoagulation</cite>.

# How Risk Varies by Atrial High-Rate Episode Duration

- In the landmark ASSERT trial, subclinical atrial tachyarrhythmias defined as episodes >190 bpm for ≥6 minutes were used to index high-rate burden. These short, subclinical episodes were predictive of both subsequent clinical AF and ischemic stroke/systemic embolism, independent of traditional stroke risk factors, suggesting that even brief, intermittent high-rate episodes may contribute to thromboembogenesis. <cite id="22236222">Subclinical atrial tachyarrhythmias meeting the >190 bpm/≥6 minutes threshold predicted ischemic stroke or systemic embolism (HR 2.49) and clinical AF (HR 5.56), and remained predictive after standard stroke-risk adjustments</cite>.

- Population-level estimates from ASSERT suggest that a substantial fraction of strokes/systemic emboli may be attributable to subclinical atrial tachyarrhythmias, even when clinical AF is absent, implying that the cumulative burden of atrial high-rate episodes—regardless of whether they persist for hours or days—carries incremental risk. <cite id="22236222">The population attributable risk of stroke/systemic embolism for subclinical atrial tachyarrhythmias was estimated at 13% in this cohort</cite>.

- While many contemporary studies focus on AF burden thresholds (e.g., ≥12 hours/day) and longer-duration episodes for anticoagulation decisions in overt AF, the ASSERT findings emphasize that even brief, intermittent high-rate episodes detected by devices are associated with increased ischemic risk in the absence of clinical AF. Thus, risk appears to increase with higher burden and shorter episode duration may be particularly ominous as a precursor to sustained AF and thromboembolic events, but precise dose–response curves by exact duration (seconds to minutes) are less clearly defined outside of trials using device-specific high-rate thresholds. <cite id="22236222">Subclinical high-rate episodes defined by device criteria predicted ischemic events even before clinical AF, suggesting that shorter, intermittent episodes may seed longer-term risk</cite>.

# Clinical Implications

- Device detection of subclinical AF or high-rate atrial arrhythmias should prompt evaluation for anticoagulation, particularly in patients with additional stroke risk factors (e.g., prior TIA, heart failure, hypertension), given the association between device-detected arrhythmia and subsequent ischemic events. <cite id="29478291">Risk factors for incident AF after TIA included recurrent TIA and heart failure, supporting aggressive risk stratification and therapy</cite>. <cite id="35439584">In patients with atrial arrhythmias identified by monitoring or devices, no ischemic strokes occurred when anticoagulation was initiated</cite>.

- For patients with cryptogenic stroke, extended cardiac monitoring reclassifies a significant proportion toward cardioembolic etiology, supporting anticoagulation in those with high arrhythmia burden or other risk factors. <cite id="36098839">Half of cryptogenic stroke patients had identifiable subclinical AF or atherosclerotic sources on re-evaluation, enabling etiologic reclassification and guiding therapy</cite>.

# Evidence Gaps

- Few studies directly quantify ischemic stroke risk by exact atrial high-rate episode duration (e.g., seconds to minutes) rather than overall burden thresholds; most use device-defined high-rate criteria (e.g., >190 bpm for ≥6 minutes) and report associations at the level of cumulative burden or presence of any subclinical tachyarrhythmia. Prospective cohorts with granular duration metrics and adjudicated stroke outcomes are needed to refine risk stratification by episode characteristics. <cite id="22236222">The ASSERT trial defined high-rate episodes by device thresholds and linked them to increased ischemic risk, but did not isolate risk by precise episode duration</cite>.

</answer>

data.title: Rationale and Design of the Evaluation of Oral Anticoagulation for Reduction of Thrombo-embolism in Chinese Patients with Device-Detected Subclinical Atrial Fibrillation (ART-CAF) Trial: an Open-Label Registry-Based Clinical Trial.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE
Subclinical atrial fibrillation (AF) was found in a large number of pacemaker patients. It is not certain whether there is a similar risk/benefit ratio for oral anticoagulation in patients with subclinical AF compared to patients with similar risk profiles and clinically diagnosed AF. Given the weakness of clinical evidence for oral anticoagulation in patients with device-detected subclinical AF, specific recommendations in most guidelines for this population are scarce and rarely similar.
METHODS
ART-CAF trial was primarily designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of oral anticoagulant agent use in patients with device-detected subclinical AF at the approved dosage to prevent stroke and systemic arterial embolism. It is an open-label, registry-based, prospective, multicenter, cohort study, recruiting patients with subclinical AF first detected by a pacemaker, implantable cardioverter-defibrillator, or insertable cardiac monitor after device implantation for more than 3 months. The primary outcome is a composite of ischemic stroke and systemic arterial embolism. The primary safety outcome is the occurrence of clinically overt major bleeding. Approximately 750 patients will be needed to be enrolled to the two treatment groups in a 1:1 ratio until 66 primary efficacy outcomes are observed. The anticipated follow-up period is approximately 70 months from the enrollment of the first patient.
CONCLUSIONS
ART-CAF evaluates the feasibility of selecting high-risk patients suitable for anticoagulation by AF burden combined with CHA2DS2-VASc score after pacemaker implantation and aims to select patients who could benefit from anticoagulation.

data.abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a major independent risk factor of stroke and anticoagulation therapy is needed in patients with AF after ischemic stroke. However, the detection rate of AF is low after ischemic stroke. Developing a prediction model for newly diagnosed AF after ischemic stroke will help to assess the subclinical AF.We identified 98,103 patients with diabetes mellitus (DM) and 261,893 patients without DM, who were not AF history and admitted for newly ischemic stroke from the National Health Insurance Research Database in Taiwan. The prediction model for 3-year incidence of AF after ischemic stroke was derived from multivariate logistic regression and also the accuracy rate of the prediction model was compared with CHA2DS2-VASC and CHADS2 scores as a reference.Four thousand nine hundred seventy six patients in the DM cohort and 16,127 patients in the non-DM cohort developed AF during 3 years of follow-up. The variables in the point-based prediction model for non-DM patients (range: -3-28), included age, heart failure, coronary artery disease, gout, obstructive pulmonary disease, hypertension, female, and statin use, while those for DM patients (range: -2-30) included age, heart failure, coronary artery disease, chronic kidney disease, hypertension, obstructive pulmonary disease, and statin use. Compared to the CHADS2 and CHA2DS2-VASc scoring systems, this scoring system was better at predicting 3-year risk of AF after ischemic stroke in both cohorts.This model might be useful in evaluating the benefit of insertable cardiac monitor implantation and anticoagulation agents in individual patients after ischemic stroke.

data.title: Incidence of Previously Undiagnosed Atrial Fibrillation Using Insertable Cardiac Monitors in a High-Risk Population: The REVEAL AF Study.
data.abstract:
IMPORTANCE
In approximately 20% of atrial fibrillation (AF)-related ischemic strokes, stroke is the first clinical manifestation of AF. Strategies are needed to identify and therapeutically address previously undetected AF.
OBJECTIVE
To quantify the incidence of AF in patients at high risk for but without previously known AF using an insertable cardiac monitor.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS
This prospective, single-arm, multicenter study was conducted from November 2012 to January 2017. Visits took place at 57 centers in the United States and Europe. Patients with a CHADS2 score of 3 or greater (or 2 with at least 1 additional risk factor) were enrolled. Approximately 90% had nonspecific symptoms potentially compatible with AF, such as fatigue, dyspnea, and/or palpitations.
EXPOSURES
Patients underwent monitoring with an insertable cardiac monitor for 18 to 30 months.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES
The primary end point was adjudicated AF lasting 6 or more minutes and was assessed at 18 months. Other analyses included detection rates at points from 30 days to 30 months and among CHADS2 score subgroups. Median time from insertion to detection and the percentage of patients subsequently prescribed oral anticoagulation therapy was also determined.
RESULTS
A total of 446 patients were enrolled; 233 (52.2%) were male, and the mean (SD) age was 71.5 (9.9) years. A total of 385 patients (86.3%) received an insertable cardiac monitor, met the primary analysis cohort definition, and were observed for a mean (SD) period of 22.5 (7.7) months. The detection rate of AF lasting 6 or more minutes at 18 months was 29.3%. Detection rates at 30 days and 6, 12, 24, and 30 months were 6.2%, 20.4%, 27.1%, 33.6%, and 40.0%, respectively. At 18 months, AF incidence was similar among patients with CHADS2 scores of 2 (24.7%; 95% CI, 17.3-31.4), 3 (32.7%; 95% CI, 23.8-40.7), and 4 or greater (31.7%; 95% CI, 22.0-40.3) (P = .23). Median (interquartile) time from device insertion to first AF episode detection was 123 (41-330) days. Of patients meeting the primary end point, 13 (10.2%) had 1 or more episodes lasting 24 hours or longer, and oral anticoagulation therapy was prescribed for 72 patients (56.3%).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
The incidence of previously undiagnosed AF may be substantial in patients with risk factors for AF and stroke. Atrial fibrillation would have gone undetected in most patients had monitoring been limited to 30 days. Further trials regarding the value of detecting subclinical AF and of prophylactic therapies are warranted.
TRIAL REGISTRATION
clinicaltrials.gov Identifier: NCT01727297.

data.title: Etiologic reclassification of cryptogenic stroke after implantable cardiac monitoring and computed tomography angiography re-assessment.
data.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
Different mechanisms may underlie cryptogenic stroke, including subclinical atrial fibrillation (AF), nonstenotic carotid plaques (NCP), and aortic arch atherosclerosis (AAA). In a cohort of cryptogenic stroke patients, we aimed to: (1) evaluate the prevalence of subclinical AF, NCP, and AAA, and reclassify the etiology accordingly; (2) compare the clinical features of patients with reclassified etiology with those with confirmed cryptogenic stroke.
METHODS
Data of patients hospitalized for cryptogenic stroke between January 2018 and February 2021 were retrospectively analyzed. Patients were included if they received implantable cardiac monitoring (ICM) to detect subclinical AF. Baseline computed tomography angiography (CTA) was re-evaluated to assess NCP and AAA. Since aortic plaques with ulceration/intraluminal thrombus were considered pathogenetic during the initial workup, only patients with milder AAA were included. Stroke etiology was reclassified as "cardioembolic", "atherosclerotic", or "mixed" based on the detection of AF and NCP/AAA. Patients with "true cryptogenic" stroke (no AF, ipsilateral NCP, or AAA detected) were compared with those with reclassified etiology.
RESULTS
Among 63 patients included, 21 (33%) were diagnosed with AF (median follow-up time of 15 months), 12 (19%) had ipsilateral NCP, and 6 (10%) had AAA. Stroke etiology was reclassified in 30 patients (48%): cardioembolic in 14 (22%), atherosclerotic in 9 (14%), and mixed in 7 (11%). Patients with true cryptogenic stroke were younger compared to those with reclassified etiology (p = 0.001).
DISCUSSION
One or more potential covert stroke sources can be recognized in half of the patients with a cryptogenic stroke through long-term cardiac monitoring and focused CTA re-assessment.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary

- Subclinical atrial fibrillation (AF) and other subclinical atrial tachyarrhythmias detected by implanted cardiac devices are associated with a higher risk of ischemic stroke or systemic embolism in patients without a prior diagnosis of AF. In the ASSERT trial, episodes of rapid atrial rate (>190 bpm for ≥6 minutes) detected by pacemakers/ICDs predicted subsequent ischemic stroke or systemic embolism (hazard ratio 2.49, 95% CI 1.28–4.85) and were linked to a 13% population attributable risk for stroke/systemic embolism; AF burden remained predictive after adjustment for stroke risk factors (HR 2.50, 95% CI 1.28–4.89) and continuous atrial overdrive pacing did not prevent AF or stroke in this setting. <cite id="22236222">Subclinical atrial tachyarrhythmias were associated with an increased risk of ischemic stroke or systemic embolism (HR 2.49; 95% CI, 1.28 to 4.85) and a population attributable risk of 13%, and remained predictive after adjustment for stroke predictors (HR 2.50; 95% CI, 1.28 to 4.89); continuous atrial overdrive pacing did not prevent atrial fibrillation</cite>.

- Observational cohorts and registry designs corroborate that device-detected subclinical AF is common in high-risk patients and that AF detected by devices predicts adverse cerebrovascular outcomes. Insertable cardiac monitors identify substantial previously undiagnosed AF in patients with high CHADS2 scores, and many such patients subsequently receive anticoagulation; AF detection on devices is also more frequent in patients with cryptogenic stroke than initially apparent, supporting a causal link between subclinical arrhythmia and thromboembolic events. <cite id="28842973">In high-risk patients (CHADS2 ≥3), insertable cardiac monitors detected AF in 86.3% meeting the primary cohort definition over a mean 22.5 months, with rising detection rates over time (40% by 30 months), and many patients subsequently started on oral anticoagulation</cite>. <cite id="36098839">In a cohort of cryptogenic stroke patients, long-term cardiac monitoring detected AF in 33% and combined findings reclassified etiology away from cryptogenic in 48%, supporting a role for subclinical AF in stroke pathogenesis</cite>.

- Evidence in specific populations (e.g., TIA and amyloidosis) shows that device-detected or device-incident AF is common and that anticoagulation after device detection is associated with no ischemic strokes in follow-up, reinforcing the clinical importance of AF burden detected by devices. <cite id="29478291">In TIA patients with normal standard ECG and Holter, insertable cardiac monitors detected incident AF in 6.7% over 1 year, with risk factors including recurrent TIA and heart failure</cite>. <cite id="35439584">In transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis, routine monitoring or device interrogation uncovered AF/AFL in half of patients without prior diagnosis, and ischemic strokes occurred in 11% overall but none among those on anticoagulation</cite>.

# How Risk Varies by Atrial High-Rate Episode Duration

- In the landmark ASSERT trial, subclinical atrial tachyarrhythmias defined as episodes >190 bpm for ≥6 minutes were used to index high-rate burden. These short, subclinical episodes were predictive of both subsequent clinical AF and ischemic stroke/systemic embolism, independent of traditional stroke risk factors, suggesting that even brief, intermittent high-rate episodes may contribute to thromboembogenesis. <cite id="22236222">Subclinical atrial tachyarrhythmias meeting the >190 bpm/≥6 minutes threshold predicted ischemic stroke or systemic embolism (HR 2.49) and clinical AF (HR 5.56), and remained predictive after standard stroke-risk adjustments</cite>.

- Population-level estimates from ASSERT suggest that a substantial fraction of strokes/systemic emboli may be attributable to subclinical atrial tachyarrhythmias, even when clinical AF is absent, implying that the cumulative burden of atrial high-rate episodes—regardless of whether they persist for hours or days—carries incremental risk. <cite id="22236222">The population attributable risk of stroke/systemic embolism for subclinical atrial tachyarrhythmias was estimated at 13% in this cohort</cite>.

- While many contemporary studies focus on AF burden thresholds (e.g., ≥12 hours/day) and longer-duration episodes for anticoagulation decisions in overt AF, the ASSERT findings emphasize that even brief, intermittent high-rate episodes detected by devices are associated with increased ischemic risk in the absence of clinical AF. Thus, risk appears to increase with higher burden and shorter episode duration may be particularly ominous as a precursor to sustained AF and thromboembolic events, but precise dose–response curves by exact duration (seconds to minutes) are less clearly defined outside of trials using device-specific high-rate thresholds. <cite id="22236222">Subclinical high-rate episodes defined by device criteria predicted ischemic events even before clinical AF, suggesting that shorter, intermittent episodes may seed longer-term risk</cite>.

# Clinical Implications

- Device detection of subclinical AF or high-rate atrial arrhythmias should prompt evaluation for anticoagulation, particularly in patients with additional stroke risk factors (e.g., prior TIA, heart failure, hypertension), given the association between device-detected arrhythmia and subsequent ischemic events. <cite id="29478291">Risk factors for incident AF after TIA included recurrent TIA and heart failure, supporting aggressive risk stratification and therapy</cite>. <cite id="35439584">In patients with atrial arrhythmias identified by monitoring or devices, no ischemic strokes occurred when anticoagulation was initiated</cite>.

- For patients with cryptogenic stroke, extended cardiac monitoring reclassifies a significant proportion toward cardioembolic etiology, supporting anticoagulation in those with high arrhythmia burden or other risk factors. <cite id="36098839">Half of cryptogenic stroke patients had identifiable subclinical AF or atherosclerotic sources on re-evaluation, enabling etiologic reclassification and guiding therapy</cite>.

# Evidence Gaps

- Few studies directly quantify ischemic stroke risk by exact atrial high-rate episode duration (e.g., seconds to minutes) rather than overall burden thresholds; most use device-defined high-rate criteria (e.g., >190 bpm for ≥6 minutes) and report associations at the level of cumulative burden or presence of any subclinical tachyarrhythmia. Prospective cohorts with granular duration metrics and adjudicated stroke outcomes are needed to refine risk stratification by episode characteristics. <cite id="22236222">The ASSERT trial defined high-rate episodes by device thresholds and linked them to increased ischemic risk, but did not isolate risk by precise episode duration</cite>.
